📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

OpenAI published its AI progress meter to encourage a slowdown. It won’t work

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that though it’s been lost amid the Jensen Huang drama at Nvidia, OpenAI made a startling revelation on Sunday.
  • Though it’s been lost amid the Jensen Huang drama at Nvidia, OpenAI made a startling revelation on Sunday.
  • Sources indicate that pachocki’s essay, titled “Perplexity and Intelligence,” includes some progress numbers that may have been meant to jolt the industry into a slowdown.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though it’s been lost amid the Jensen Huang drama at Nvidia, OpenAI made a startling revelation on Sunday. In an essay, the firm’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, made an overture to rival AI labs to agree on ways to slow down the development of fresh models. But with billions at stake and companies racing for enterprise customers, there’s little reason to believe anyone will hit the brakes. Pachocki’s essay, titled “Perplexity and Intelligence,” includes some progress numbers that may have been meant to jolt the industry into a slowdown. He discloses for the first time an internal metric that OpenAI uses to track how much its models improve during pretraining. Pachocki invites other frontier AI labs to publish comparable numbers, creating a common basis for monitoring—and potentially coordinating a slowdown in—the development of artificial intelligence until adequate safety and monitoring tools can be developed. OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, praised the essay, going on X to call it “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.” Microsoft AI’s CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, voiced his company’s support for the effort and reported a progress score for one of its own models. Pachocki’s proposal, however, is unlikely to matter if the other labs don’t publish their own progress numbers and agree to speed limits. And so far, other labs, including Anthropic and Google DeepMind, have not signaled a willingness to sign on. An alarming acceleration Pachocki has good reason to propose a pause. OpenAI’s numbers show AI advancing at an alarmingly fast rate. OpenAI’s own progress score improved more in 2026 than in the previous three years combined, Pachocki indicates, and an unreleased internal model highlights another large stride in intelligence. The numbers OpenAI published are “perplexity” scores, which measure how confidently a language model predicts the next word in unfamiliar text. Researchers test models on withheld data, with lower scores indicating more confident predictions and a log-perplexity score of zero meaning the model assigns 100% probability to every correct token. (Yes, the AI search company Perplexity was, sadly, named after this metric.) Since 2022, OpenAI’s base-model log-perplexity has fallen from roughly 0.99 (capable of “fluent conversation”) to 0.76 (capable of solving “a Millennium Prize math problem”)—a striking improvement in how well models predict tokens, which can represent words, numbers, code, etc. The chart’s biggest story may concern what comes after current frontier models. OpenAI’s most recent model, GPT-6.2 Astra, reaches a score of 0.76, while an unreleased internal model has already dropped to a score of 0.73, OpenAI says—a conspicuous break from the earlier pace of progress. Pachocki’s essay comes on the heels of a claim by the Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge that Claude helped him prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, a famous unsolved problem in mathematics. Earlier this year, OpenAI’s own models solved a series of exceptionally difficult math problems. But also, the company’s AI agents broke out of their testing environment this summer and infiltrated servers at Hugging Face, an AI collaboration platform, looking for ways to cheat on a math task. And AI models have advanced rapidly in computer coding and cyber capabilities this year, as well as in their ability to develop new AI models. A decent proposal Pachocki asks frontier developers to set shared norms for evaluating and red-teaming models before release and to commit to common limits, based on perplexity and other measures, that no one crosses until monitoring reaches a concrete milestone. Today, AI labs use a kind of monitoring tool to track a reasoning model’s chain of thought, or the logical steps the model takes to reach a conclusion or action. Pachocki suggests developing a new kind of monitoring tool to keep pace with improvements in perplexity. And that’s one of the problems. The AI labs use different testing metrics and training data mixes, so imposing a shared limit on lowering perplexity scores would first require a common way of measuring perplexity: a shared test. Also, because perplexity alone doesn’t capture gains from reasoning and reinforcement learning, a lab could keep its base model within the agreed limits and still ship a far more capable product. Coordination has already run into the law—antitrust law. After Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, called for labs to slow down earlier this year, OpenAI’s policy chief, Chris Lehane, said OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google had been talking about safety for weeks. Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, said there was “no world” in which he would grant them an antitrust exemption. On September 18, paying consumers of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini sued the four companies behind them, alleging an illegal agreement to slow AI development. A shared perplexity floor could invite that same kind of reaction. Perverse incentives But the biggest barrier—and the elephant in the room that makes all this seem performative—is the massive economic incentive to speed ahead with AI model development. All the major AI labs are under pressure to continue driving up revenues to offset the massive capital expenditures needed to develop and operate frontier models. By this time next year, all the major AI labs could be public companies, their stock prices subject to the revenues they report every quarter. The best way for the labs to keep revenues growing is to hold on to their existing customers and attract new ones. Since the pool of customers is finite, the major labs must compete for those customers. The best way to do that is by releasing ever more capable models as rapidly as possible. So increasing model capability is rewarded, and safety research is seen as a cost of doing business. The only way slowing down makes sense is if all AI labs participate. Perhaps a government entity could help the AI labs agree on their measurements and slowdown terms. Amodei explicitly pointed to the Federal Aviation Administration as a model for AI regulation and government oversight that includes third-party evaluations of powerful models. This is unlikely, at least during the next two years, because the Trump administration’s alliance with the tech industry is built on a commitment to leave the AI labs to regulate themselves. The administration has even tried several times to preempt states from regulating AI. One of the main arguments for leaving the AI industry unregulated is the narrative that slowing down AI R&D is bad for the U.S. because it would open the door for China to take the lead. China, then, would be the country dictating technological standards to the world and perhaps using its AI dominance in military applications as leverage against other countries. Still, Trump said Friday that the U.S. would work with China on “joint guardrails” for AI, Semafor reported. Give Pachocki credit for doing something new. Through his essay, OpenAI showed competitors where it stands in a way no other lab has done. Credit Microsoft for showing that labs can compare base models on a shared test. If the other major labs follow suit, it would be a major step toward the industry’s working together to pace AI development and ensure adequate safety standards.

#172255. Gratitude changes how we see the world. And that changes everything, including your team’s performance

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Gratitude changes how we see the world. And that changes everything, including your team’s performance

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in 1863, as the United States was at risk of splitting apart in a bloody civil war, President Abraham Lincoln called on Americans to give thanks.
  • In 1863, as the United States was at risk of splitting apart in a bloody civil war, President Abraham Lincoln called on Americans to give thanks.
  • The war was in its third year, and the Battle of Gettysburg had left more than 50,000 soldiers wounded, missing, or dead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 1863, as the United States was at risk of splitting apart in a bloody civil war, President Abraham Lincoln called on Americans to give thanks. The war was in its third year, and the Battle of Gettysburg had left more than 50,000 soldiers wounded, missing, or dead. The country’s future was entirely uncertain, people in Northern and Southern states were deeply divided—and yet on October 3, Lincoln issued a proclamation designating the last Thursday of November as a national day of Thanksgiving. Sarah Josepha Hale, the writer and activist, had been urging U.S. presidents to do this for decades without success, until that moment. Considering the physical, emotional, and psychological toll the war was having on the American people, it’s remarkable that Lincoln believed the nation still had blessings worth counting, even when people had every reason to focus on what was going wrong. That distinction gets to the heart of why gratitude matters, not just at Thanksgiving, but throughout our daily lives. Gratitude Changes What We See Feeling grateful comes easily in the massive events of life—when we get a promotion, buy our first home, or receive a clean bill of health after a harrowing illness. But as Lincoln seemed to understand, gratitude may be most valuable when our lives are off track or not going in the direction we’d hoped. When we acknowledge the good around us, we begin to see our circumstances differently. Rather than becoming consumed by what’s missing or going wrong, we recognize that there is always much in our lives worth appreciating. Human beings are naturally drawn to outliers, things that interfere with our happiness: our problems, challenges and anything requiring fixing. That attention can serve a useful motivational purpose, but when it dominates our thinking, we can lose sight of what is working; all we’ve achieved and the people who enrich and enable our lives. Gratitude doesn’t require us to ignore what’s wrong. It opens us up to seeing the bigger picture. In doing so, it can shift us from negativity and disappointment toward a more positive, hopeful and optimistic view of our lives. More than a century and a half later, psychology would confirm what Lincoln seemed to know intuitively: Directing our attention toward what’s good in our lives doesn’t deny hardship, but it can meaningfully shape how we experience it. Research has found that people who practice gratitude tend to be more optimistic, more resilient, and better able to maintain a sense of well-being during difficult times. Being Grateful Doesn’t Mean Everything Is Good Oliver Sacks, the British neurologist and best-selling author, offered a striking illustration of this distinction near the end of his life. In his short collection of essays, Gratitude, he reflected on his terminal cancer diagnosis and the knowledge that his time on the planet was running out. Even facing death, he wrote, “I cannot pretend I am without fear. But my predominant feeling is one of gratitude.” That admission is stunning because Sacks wasn’t denying the reality of his circumstances or suggesting he should be thankful for dying. Instead, he was expressing gratitude for the life he’d led, including the books he’d written, his scientific work, his relationships, and all the experiences over the years that had brought him happiness. David Steindl-Rast, an author and Benedictine monk who is globally recognized as the “grandfather of gratitude,” makes a similar distinction. We cannot reasonably be grateful for everything that happens to us, but we can find opportunities for gratitude amid our hardships and clearly see all that remains valuable. Gratitude simply allows us to recognize both realities without letting either one erase the other. What Gratitude Means for Leaders As workplace leaders are generally responsible for meeting goals and completing projects, they’re naturally motivated to identify where their teams are falling short so they can turn things around in time. Those obligations demand attention, but they can also build a habit of zeroing in exclusively on performance gaps. When leaders lose sight of their teams’ wins, they risk discouraging future successes by leaving employees feeling their boss can never be satisfied. Consistent with this, research from Gallup and Workhuman found in 2024 that only 22% of employees say they receive the right amount of appreciation for their work. And this directly affects more than morale; it impacts productivity. Compelling organizational psychology studies also show that gratitude acts as a powerful catalyst as more appreciated employees demonstrate higher resilience, greater intrinsic motivation, and significantly greater results. Expressing gratitude provides a counterbalance. A leader who openly and frequently recognizes their employees’ abilities, appreciates the effort behind their accomplishments, and acknowledges the team for overcoming challenges demonstrates that they not only see but also appreciate the people and relationships that make their successes possible. Research published in the Journal of Applied Psychology in 2026 found that gratitude expressed by leaders often prompted employees to notice and express appreciation toward their coworkers, strengthening relationships within the organization. That finding suggests that gratitude can influence more than the relationship between a leader and employee; it can help shape how people treat one another, fostering a greater sense of belonging and well-being within a team. A Practice, Not a Holiday Lincoln’s Thanksgiving proclamation came in the midst of the Civil War, not after the strife was over. And while gratitude didn’t erase the division or bring the nation back together overnight, it offered Americans a reason to appreciate all that remained worth preserving. In our own lives, we face great losses, disappointments and frustrations—and there will always be things we wish were different. But by dwelling only on what’s missing, we risk overlooking the people who enrich us, the daily experiences that bring us joy, and all the progress we’ve made. Gratitude widens our aperture and gives us a richer interpretation of things. Thanksgiving Day provides an annual reminder to be grateful, but the greater opportunity is to make gratitude part of how we see the world every day of the year and, in doing so, make our lives far more expansive.

According to recent reports, research published in the Journal of Applied Psychology in 2026 found that gratitude expressed by leaders often prompted employees to notice and express appreciation toward their coworkers, strengthening relationships within the organization. That finding suggests that gratitude can influence more than the relationship between a leader and employee; it can help shape how people treat one another, fostering a greater sense of belonging and well-being within a team.

Lincoln’s Thanksgiving proclamation came in the midst of the Civil War, not after the strife was over. And while gratitude didn’t erase the division or bring the nation back together overnight, it offered Americans a reason to appreciate all that remained worth preserving.

In a recent development, in our own lives, we face great losses, disappointments and frustrations—and there will always be things we wish were different. But by dwelling only on what’s missing, we risk overlooking the people who enrich us, the daily experiences that bring us joy, and all the progress we’ve made. Gratitude widens our aperture and gives us a richer interpretation of things.

Thanksgiving Day provides an annual reminder to be grateful, but the greater opportunity is to make gratitude part of how we see the world every day of the year and, in doing so, make our lives far more expansive.

Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL.
  • We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.
  • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL. We used MCPs "Streamable HTTP" transport for deployment, and examine in detail the trade-offs that Server Developers have.

We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.

At Hugging Face, providing access to the Hub via MCP is an obvious choice, and this article shares our experience developing the hf.co/mcp MCP Server.

The community uses the Hub for research, development, content creation and more. We wanted to let people customize the server for their own needs, as well as easily access thousands of AI applications available on Spaces. This meant making the MCP Server dynamic by adjusting consumers' tools on the fly.

We also wanted to make access simple by avoiding complicated downloads and configuration, so making it remotely accessible via a simple URL was a must.

It has been revealed that when building a remote MCP Server, the first decision is deciding how clients will connect to it. MCP offers several transport options, with different trade-offs. TL;DR: our open source code supports all variants, but for production we chose to go with the most modern one. This section goes through the different options in detail.

Industry observers note that since its launch in November 2024, MCP has undergone rapid evolution with 3 protocol revisions in 9 months. This has seen the replacement of the SSE Transport with Streamable HTTP, as well as the introduction and rework of authorization.

These rapid changes mean support for different MCP Features and revisions in Client applications varies, providing extra challenges for our design choices.

Here is a brief summary of the Transport Options offered by the Model Context Protocol and associated SDKs:.

Both STDIO and HTTP with SSE are fully bi-directional by default - meaning that Client and Server maintain an open connection and can send messages to each other at any time.

SSE refers to "Server Sent Events" - a way for HTTP Servers to maintain an open connection and send events in response to a request.

MCP Server Developers face a lot of choices when setting up the Streamable HTTP transport.

There are 3 main communication patterns to choose from:.

When using Request Scoped Streams with the official SDKs, use the sendNotification() and sendRequest() methods provided in the RequestHandlerExtra parameter (TypeScript) or set the related_request_id (Python) to send messages to the correct stream.

An additional factor to consider is whether or not the MCP Server itself needs to maintain state for each connection. This is decided by the Server when the Client sends its Initialize request:.

The table below summarizes the MCP Features and their supported communication pattern:.

With Request Scoped streams, Sampling and Elicitation requests need a Stateful connection so that the mcp-session-id can be used for response association.

The Hugging Face MCP Server is Open Source - and supports STDIO, SSE and Streamable HTTP deployment in both Direct Response and Server Push mode. You can configure keep-alive and last activity timeouts when using Server Push Streams. There's also a built-in observability dashboard that you can use to understand how different Clients manage connections, and handle Tool List change notifications.

The following picture demonstrates our MCP Server connection dashboard running in "Server Push" Streamable HTTP mode:.

For production, we decided to launch our MCP Server with Streamable HTTP in a Stateless, Direct Response configuration for the following reasons:.

Industry observers note that stateless For anonymous owners we supply a standard set of Tools for using the Hub along with an Image Generator. For authenticated users our state comprises their selected tools and chosen Gradio applications. We also make sure that users ZeroGPU quota is correctly applied for their account. This is managed using the supplied HF_TOKEN or OAuth credentials that we look up on request. None of our existing tools require us to maintain any other state between requests.

Sources indicate that you can use OAuth login by adding ?login to the MCP Server url - e.g. https://huggingface.co/mcp?login. We may make this the default once the claude.ai remote integration supports the latest OAuth spec.

Direct Response provides the lowest deployment resource overhead - and we don't at the moment have any Tools that require Sampling or Elicitation during execution.

Future Support At launch, the "HTTP with SSE" transport was still the remote default in a lot of MCP Clients. However, we didn't want to invest heavily in managing it due to its imminent deprecation. Fortunately, popular clients had already started making the switch (VSCode and Cursor), and within a week of launch claude.ai also added support. If you need to connect with SSE, feel free to deploy a copy of our Server on a FreeCPU Hugging Face Space.

In a recent development, in the future, we would like to support real-time Tool List Changed notifications when people update their settings on the Hub. However, this raises a couple of practical issues:.

It has been revealed that first, people tend to configure their favourite MCP Servers in their Client and leave them enabled. This means that the Client remains connected whilst the application is open. Sending notifications would mean maintaining as many open connections as there were currently active Clients - regardless of active usage - on the chance the user updates their tool configuration.

Sources indicate that second, most MCP Servers and Clients disconnect after a period of inactivity, resuming when necessary. This inevitably means that immediate push notifications would be missed - as the notification channel will have been closed. In practice, it is far simpler for the Client to refresh the connection and Tool List as needed.

Unless you have reasonable control over the Client/Server pair, using Server Push Streams adds a lot of complexity to a public deployment, when lower-resource solutions for refreshing the Tool List exist.

Just before launch, @julien-c submitted a PR to include friendly instructions for users visiting hf.co/mcp. This hugely improves the User Experience - the default response is otherwise an unfriendly bit of JSON.

Initially, we found this generated an enormous amount of traffic. After a bit of investigation we found that when returning a web page rather than an HTTP 405 error, VSCode would poll the endpoint multiple times per second!

In a recent development, the fix suggested by @coyotte508 was to properly detect browsers and only return the page in that circumstance. Thanks also to the VSCode team who rapidly fixed it.

Although not specifically stated - returning a page in this manner does seem acceptable within the MCP Specification.

The MCP Protocol sends several requests during initialization. A typical connection sequence is: Initialize, Notifications/Initialize, tools/list and then prompts/list.

Given that MCP Clients will connect and reconnect whilst open, and the fact that owners make periodic calls, we find there is a ratio of around 100 MCP Control messages for each Tool Call.

Some clients also send requests that don't make sense for our Stateless, Direct Response configuration - for example Pings, Cancellations or attempts to list Resources (which isn't a capability we currently advertise).

In a recent development, the first week of July 2025 saw an astonishing 164 different Clients accessing our Server. Interestingly, one of the most popular tools is mcp-remote. Approximately half of all Clients use it as a bridge to connect to our remote server.

MCP is rapidly evolving, and we're excited about what has already been achieved across Chat Applications, IDEs, Agents and MCP Servers over the last few months.

We can already see how powerful integrating the Hugging Face Hub has been and support for Gradio Spaces now makes it possible for LLMs to be easily extended with the latest Machine Learning applications.

Here are some great examples of things people have been doing with our MCP Server so far:.

We hope that this post has provided insights to the decisions that need to be made building Remote MCP Servers, and encourage you to try some of the examples in your favourite MCP Client.

Take a look at our Open Source MCP Server, and try some of the different transport options with your Client, or open an Issue or Pull Request to make improvements or suggest upcoming functionality.

Let us know your thoughts, feedback and questions on this discussion thread.

TL;DR: ScreenEnv is a powerful Python library that lets you create isolated Ubuntu desktop environments in Docker containers for testing and deploying GUI Agents (aka Computer Use agents). With built-in support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it's never been easier to deploy desktop agents that can see, click, and interact with real applications.

It has been revealed that imagine you need to automate desktop tasks, test GUI applications, or build an AI agent that can interact with software. This used to require complex VM setups and brittle automation frameworks.

ScreenEnv changes this by providing a sandboxed desktop environment that runs in a Docker container. Think of it as a complete virtual desktop session that your code can fully control - not just clicking buttons and typing text, but managing the entire desktop experience including launching applications, organizing windows, handling files, executing terminal commands, and recording the entire session.

This dual approach means ScreenEnv adapts to your existing infrastructure rather than forcing you to change your agent architecture.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

Sources indicate that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

Industry observers note that there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

It has been revealed that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

It has been revealed that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

It has been revealed that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

It has been revealed that store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Industry observers note that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

According to recent reports, every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

It has been revealed that the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Sources indicate that now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Industry observers note that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

According to recent reports, A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

According to recent reports, in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Tech Report: Asynchronous Robot Inference: Decoupling Action Prediction and Execution

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action.
  • Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.
  • Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action. This results in the robot being idle while awaiting upcoming actions to perform, introducing noticeable lags at execution, and lacking responsiveness. Asynchronous inference tightens the control loop, removing lags at runtime and resulting in more adaptive control by decoupling action prediction from action execution. In this blog post, we cover the basics behind async inference, and how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies in the real-world.

Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.

Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second). Allowing for replanning and a tighter control loop, async inference results in (1) attempts at recovery, and (2) a ~2x speedup in task completion. Sequential inference keeps acting out the current action chunk even after failure to grasp the object, while async inference can replan and act the upcoming action chunk. Both setups use the same policy!

Sources indicate that with async inference, we decouple action execution from action prediction. This is particularly relevant considering the tendency of currently popular models like [ACT], [OpenVLA], [PI0], and [SmolVLA] to be outputting chunks of actions at:t+Ha_{t:t+H}at:t+H​ rather than single actions ata_tat​ given an observation oto_tot​. Convince yourself of this by running all these models using LeRobot.

It has been revealed that using chunks sequentially results in (1) lags at runtime, impacting task execution time and (2) lack of responsiveness, due to acting widely open-loop. Asynchronous inference mitigates both these limitations by decoupling action prediction from action execution. We introduced asynchronous inference in SmolVLA, and found it to result in a ~2x speed-up in task completion time with comparable task success rate.

In particular, we design a 2-component system where policy inference and action execution are performed in two different processes, possibly on two different machines connected through the network:.

Communication between PolicyServer and RobotClient relies on gRPC, which guarantees ~5× faster performance than a comparable REST API. The result of all of this is a robot that never waits for inference.

Asynchronous inference, highlighting: (1) The client sending the first observation for inference, receiving the first chunk shortly after; (2) The client sending another observation for processing while it has not yet exhausted the current chunk; (3) The client receiving an updated action chunk, which it aggregates with the remainders of the one it was previously executing.

It has been revealed that suppose a policy π \pi π maps the current observation ot o_t ot​ to a sequence of H H H future actions. Formally, π:O  ↦  A,At=(at,at+1,…at+H)=π(ot)\pi : \mathcal{O} \;\mapsto\; \mathcal{A}, \mathbf{A}_t = \begin{pmatrix} a_{t}, & a_{t+1}, & \dots & a_{t+H} \end{pmatrix} = \pi(o_t)π:O↦A,At​=(at​,​at+1​,​…​at+H​​)=π(ot​).

A traditional control loop would therefore consist of the following steps:.

During step 2 the robot is idle. The latency grows with the model size (and models tend to be increasingly bulky over time), and can swiftly dominate interaction time (which is typically around 1/fps), as shown in the video below (coming from our Discord community 🤗):.

This directly results in (1) reduced performance in terms of task completion time---the robot needs to be waiting for the next action chunk to be computed---and (2) reduced responsiveness, due to (2.1) acting widely open-loop while actions are available and (2.2) complete idleness while waiting for the next action chunk.

In a recent development, (Left)Sequential inference with highlighted idle periods. (Right)Time to select an action showing spikes when inference is triggered due to local queue exhaustion (inference latency is around ~100ms---~3 frames at 30fps---using an ACT model on a 2021 MacBook Pro).

Our system removes the idle period by overlapping computation and execution:.

The key idea is that the robot already knows what to do for the next few timesteps, so it can keep moving while fresh actions are being computed on the server.

Asynchronous inference overlaps in time the execution of the current action chunk with the computation of the next one, by decoupling these two processes, possibly running them on entirely distinct machines connected through the network.

This results in a tighter control loop, and a robot that never waits for inference. In turn, this results in ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop (see video below).

Because gRPC is HTTP/2-based and uses protocol buffers, it achieves low-latency binary messaging and bidirectional streams out of the box, which in turn helps us maintain a tighter control loop and sub-100ms round-trip latency (on our local network, and hosting SmolVLA on a NVIDIA RTX 4090).

The RobotClient runs on-board, and streams observations to the PolicyServer through gRPC. The PolicyServer prepares the observations received for inference, and sends back to the RobotClient an action chunk.

According to recent reports, from the client's perspective, observations are streamed to the server according to the local queue status. Incoming chunks are aggregated on overlapping portions with the presently available action queue.

It has been revealed that the RobotClient maintains a local action queue and follows a simple yet effective strategy: send a upcoming observation when the queue length drops below a configurable threshold (\(g\) in the SmolVLA paper, chunk_size_threshold in the code). This threshold value, expressed as a fraction of the maximum chunk size, acts as a trigger condition that balances computational load with responsiveness.

The client streams observations to the server, according to the local queue status.

From the client's perspective, the process unfolds as follows:.

Sources indicate that queue monitoring: The client continuously monitors its action queue length against a chunk size threshold parameter. When the queue drops below this threshold, it signals that a new observation should be sent for processing.

According to recent reports, observation streaming: Once the threshold condition is met, the client captures the current observation and streams it to the PolicyServer via gRPC. Crucially, observations are streamed rather than being sent via a unary RPC because they typically exceed the maximum message size of 4MB (multiple camera captures at high resolution result in this).

It has been revealed that action chunk aggregation: When a upcoming action chunk arrives from the server, the client merges it with any remaining actions in the current queue over the overlapping portion. This is where custom aggregators come into play, handling overlapping sections between the current and incoming chunks differently. As of now, we support flexibly aggregation between the chunks via the specification of a custom aggregate_fn(chunk1: torch.Tensor, chunk2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor function, which is called for each overlapping timestep and can be user-provided. The overlapping portions (shown in light blue in the diagram) require careful handling. We can design different aggregation strategies:.

This system is highly configurable, as the chunk size threshold can be tuned based on network latency, model inference time, and desired responsiveness. A lower threshold means more frequent updates (and higher computational cost), while a higher threshold reduces communication overhead at the expense of potential queue starvation. Lastly, we typically receive actions from PolicyServer in a thread, and perform them in another one. This keeps the client listening for incoming chunks in a separate thread, without blocking execution and always consuming the current chunk until a new one becomes fully available.

Upon receiving observations from the RobotClient, the PolicyServer receives observations from the RobotClient, and performs the necessary observation cleaning to make received observations ready for inference. This process is illustrated in the image below:.

The observation cleaning pipeline running on the server, highlighting the three main steps related to (1) Keys matching (2) Preprocessing and (3) Preparation for inference.

Once the observation has been prepared, it is compared with the last observation used for inference. This avoids collapsing into a loop whereby very similar observations are processed, thus triggering unnecessary inference and similar actions being executed (which in turn, result in very similar observations being processed again). We compare observations in terms of their joint-space similarity, which provides us an approximate and quick way of measuring changes in the robot. Clearly, this metric is not adaptive to dynamic changes in the environment (an object changing its position, or disturbances being applied), but we found it to be a good trade-off for the majority of the cases, and to be very effective in avoiding unnecessary inference and state collapse. Critically, the RobotClient retains control over whether a given observation must be processed, to avoid deadlocks. Observations sent by the client and tagged with must_go=True are processed regardless of the similarity metric.

The policy workflow, in which incoming observations are compared to the last one used for inference, and processed only if different enough, or `must_go`.

Lastly, to ensure the PolicyServer always processes the latest available observation, we block incoming observations until the previous one has been successfully processed. In this, we leverage queues on the PolicyServer to ensure incoming observations are not enqueued until the server is ready to process them (see below).

The client pings the server every 1/fps seconds, but observations are not enqueued for processing until the previous one has been successfully processed.

For all practical purposes, in async inference there are two time-scales that matter:.

Importantly, the ratio c=environment_dtinference_time c = \frac{\texttt{environment\_dt}}{\texttt{inference\_time}} c=inference_timeenvironment_dt​ results in different behaviours:.

Critically, ccc influences the number of available actions in the queue at any given time. To avoid the aforementioned sequential limit control, one can:.

Industry observers note that experiments (see plots below) show that g≈0.7g\approx0.7g≈0.7 offers a good trade-off when observations sent are not filtered out (they are all must-go). We recommend setting g=0.5g=0.5g=0.5 and following our documentation to tune this parameter to your needs.

Recent findings suggest that the number of available actions in the queue at any given time, as a function of g. Larger values of g result in more frequent updates, and more computational cost. Values of g closer to 0 reproduce sequential inference (empty queue, wait). We found g~0.7 to be a good trade-off in our experiments.

In a recent development, async inference is a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

According to recent reports, to run your policy using async inference, you just need to follow our tutorial with your own custom parameters (e.g., the policy path or the chunk size threshold). Async inference comes with support for policies supporting action chunking!

We have introduced async inference, a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

We are excited to share this work with the community, and to see how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies. We welcome PRs to improve and extend the async inference framework at huggingface/lerobot, and are available to discuss this further in our Discord community, 🤗.

Came across this while I was working on something similar. Good work.

According to recent reports, I built Inferential to handle multi-robot inference orchestration on Ray Serve. Deadline-aware scheduling scores requests across cadence urgency (EMA-tracked), robot-reported priority, anti-starvation age, trajectory progress, and static priority. ZMQ ROUTER/DEALER transport with protobuf+numpy wire format -- under 1ms serialize-transmit-deserialize vs ~100ms over gRPC. Request TTL, overflow policies, automatic disconnect detection, dispatch retry.

Will try to benchmark Inferential as well.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that youTube channel Budget-Builds Official has done the unthinkable, getting Grand Theft Auto V to run on a Radeon graphics card from 2007 with just 64MB of VRAM.
  • The channel detailed the feat, which targets a GPU with just a sixteenth of the video memory that’s usually required to play the game.
  • In a recent development, in fact, the chosen card, an ATI Radeon HD 2350, is potentially the worst card that can launch GTA V, at least by the tester’s claim, even though its DDR2 memory is probably one of the few types not in short supply at the moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that youTube channel Budget-Builds Official has done the unthinkable, getting Grand Theft Auto V to run on a Radeon graphics card from 2007 with just 64MB of VRAM. The game is almost downright playable, too, with config edits, a move to Windows 8, and an overclock getting its speed up from just 1 FPS into the 13 to 20 FPS range, sans most cars, that is.

The channel detailed the feat, which targets a GPU with just a sixteenth of the video memory that’s usually required to play the game. GTA V Legacy lists, as its minimum, an Nvidia 9800 GT or AMD HD 4870, both cards with DirectX 10 support and 1GB of VRAM. The Enhanced version, released in 2025, needs 4GB, from a GTX 1630 or RX 6400 as specified.

In a recent development, in fact, the chosen card, an ATI Radeon HD 2350, is potentially the worst card that can launch GTA V, at least by the tester’s claim, even though its DDR2 memory is probably one of the few types not in short supply at the moment. Notably, this approach doesn’t involve using a unified or shared system memory AMD APU workaround; this is dedicated VRAM. It’s also not the first attempt at something like this, as the channel has an earlier run with 8MB of VRAM on games like Half-Life 2 and Minecraft.

In a recent development, reaching the final settings took “the best part of half a day” of tweaking, after which it was possible to complete the prologue and the first mission. In some respects, the end result “genuinely does look like a PS2 game,” which probably wouldn’t actually faze fans of the series. However, for this specific title, the modder believes that “this is as low as you can actually go with GTA V.” Going any lower would likely mean reimagining the game in some way.

Sources indicate that the game’s first launch with the card, on Windows 10 and the Catalyst 13.1 driver, led to a start screen hang of about 10 minutes. The game was expecting the previous HD 6900-series card, and a settings deletion plus relaunch got things back into action. One of the video’s chapter titles, “We are in GAME... at 1FPS,” summarizes the experience pretty well.

The plan was to use the lowest in-menu settings, of course, and then the config file from the channel’s earlier 256MB run with various settings: no shadows, no reflections, and a resolution around 240p. This got things to 3 FPS, a significant improvement, but far from good enough. Changes to level-of-detail values to their lowest levels got things up to 10 FPS. However, it wasn’t yet time to give up.

Downgrading to Windows 8 and Catalyst 12.6, “the original display drivers for Windows 8,” as well as an older build of the game, paved the pathway forward. Importantly, the OS exposed overclocking that wasn’t available in Windows 10, so a second fan went onto the card first, and the GPU’s core was pushable from 400MHz to 520MHz with the assistance of MSI Afterburner. Pushing the memory from 400MHz to 475MHz led to a black screen, and the video doesn’t say what the memory ended up at, though the card survived.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Windows 8 setup reached 14 FPS, and further engine-file edits, to visual settings.dat and to level-of-detail options through OpenIV, put gameplay in the 13 to 20 FPS range.

Ignore the dots on the screen during gameplay; the tester indicates these are from being out of memory, verified by an artifact-free Unigine Valley run.

The game ended up playable, although, aside from the dots, it had many other visual complications: gaps between vertices in the world, and side characters had far fewer textures than the main ones. Additionally, most cars didn’t render, since keeping them loaded crashed the game with out-of-memory errors. This makes police “hover” into scenes and, hilariously, pop out of invisible cars. Likewise, the train in the prologue never actually loads. First-person driving, at least, works. All of this plays within that range, although busier city streets can drop from 15 down to 11 or 12 FPS.

The creator says the full gameplay will likely go up as its own video on a second channel, in “lossless quality.” The video is timely, acting as a send-off just before GTA VI’s release on Nov. 19, although not yet on PC, with a PC version reportedly due next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EEG machines are used to detect and record brain activity, so one enterprising tech enthusiast decided to use them to play GTA VI. Creator Perri Karyal demonstrated her feat on X, where she streamed her gameplay while wearing a wireless electroencephalogram (EEG) designed for research.

It has been revealed that I STOLE A JET WITH MIND CONTROL IN GTA6 this took me AGES you have no idea what should I do next?? This electroencephalogram (EEG) records my brain activity and when I'm imagining something I've trained the software to recognise (like pushing a cube forward), a button will be pressed on my virtual xbox controller. For this run, I was imagining pushing a boulder to accelerate, getting angry to interact with vehicles, and imagining a cricket hopping to jump. I use eyetracking and gyro for joysticks :)November 22, 2026.

According to recent reports, perri could be seen jumping a fence with Jason on a motorbike, before proceeding toward a parked fighter to steal and fly it. Her brain activity is overlaid on the screen while she’s playing, and viewers could also see the creator intensely focused on the game.

Industry observers note that she trained the software to recognize specific brain signals and mapped them to an action on her Xbox controller. For example, imagining pushing a cube forward would correspond to a button press, getting angry lets her interact with cars and other vehicles, while picturing a hopping cricket would also make her character jump. The joysticks, on the other hand, are controlled via eye tracking and through gyroscopes on the head unit.

While Perri makes it look effortless, using the EEG device for gaming is way harder than what many people think. “People don’t realize how challenging it is!” Karyal replied to a comment. One viewer also mentioned the huge mass of brainwaves that appeared on the screen when she took off on the jet, to which she responded, “I was so stressed out. DO YOU KNOW HOW MANY TIMES I TRIED TO DO THIS.” Even though using wireless EEG for gaming does not have any apparent side effects, the creator said that she gets headaches after hours of gaming because of how much the headset squeezes her head.

This isn’t the first time that we’ve seen people playing games using just their mind. Neuralink has recently shown off one of its patients shooting at NPCs and even “threading the needle” with a speedboat using a brain-computer interface (BCI) chip. The big difference between Perri’s creation and Neuralink’s BCI, though, is that the latter requires invasive neurosurgery.

According to recent reports, it may be surprising to think how a tech creator could beat Neuralink at its own game, but the latter has already applied the technology to multiple trial patients. We’ve seen them playing complicated games like World of Warcraft and Counter-Strike 2, while others used it for productivity and creativity, like editing a YouTube video.

It has been revealed that these technologies are still in the development and trial phases or are being experimented on by enterprising creators and tech tubers. However, it also gives hope to individuals with limited mobility, as it gives them hope that they could regain some form of mobility and independence in the future.

Kimina-Prover: Applying Test-time RL Search on Large Formal Reasoning Models

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2].
  • Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.
  • Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2]. Alongside it, we are also releasing two distilled variants: Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and 1.7B (based on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-1.7B[3] respectively).

Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.

Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.

According to recent reports, these advancements enable Kimina-Prover to solve challenging mathematical problems and surpass prior methods. As shown in Figure 1, on the widely used miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a state-of-the-art pass rate of 92.2%.

Recent findings suggest that we focus on automated theorem proving (ATP) in the Lean 4 language, aiming to automate the construction of formal mathematical proofs. Recent advances in neural theorem proving have significantly improved the ability of AI systems to assist with or automate this process. Notable progress includes AlphaProof[4] from Google DeepMind, which demonstrated strong performance on problems at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Open-source systems such as DeepSeek-Prover-V2[5], which incorporates reinforcement learning, have also achieved state-of-the-art results. In addition, neuro-symbolic agentic approaches like DSP+[6] have shown that competitive performance is possible without large-scale training by leveraging off-the-shelf models in a modular framework.

Recent findings suggest that our earlier work of Kimina-Prover Preview[7] introduced a large language model for formal theorem proving in Lean, establishing a upcoming performance baseline on the miniF2F benchmark. Trained with a large-scale reinforcement learning pipeline, the model adopted a reasoning-driven exploration paradigm and demonstrated that larger models can serve as stronger formal reasoners. Its structured reasoning pattern enabled efficient proof search and emulated human-like problem-solving strategies.

Following this initial success, we continued to improve the model through further iterations of reinforcement learning. However, single-step reasoning remains insufficient for solving complex problems that require long, multi-stage proofs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework, which enables the model to discover, combine, and reuse multiple intermediate lemmas autonomously. This framework supports deeper, long-horizon reasoning by decomposing hard problems into reusable subcomponents.

It has been revealed that A key ingredient of TTRL search is the lemma-enabled pattern, which allows the model to identify and apply intermediate lemmas as part of its proof construction process. This structured reuse of intermediate results significantly expands the model’s problem-solving capability beyond single-step generation.

To further enhance robustness, we also integrate an error-fixing mechanism that interprets Lean’s error messages and proposes targeted corrections. This allows the model to refine its outputs through iterative feedback, improving proof reliability and overall sample efficiency.

As the combination of the proposed techniques results in significant improvements in formal theorem proving performance. On the miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a pass rate of 84.0% with pass@32 and 86.4% with the addition of a single round of error correction. With pass@1024, the pass rate reaches 87.7%. Applying the full Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework yields a final pass rate of 92.2%, with an estimated pass upper bound of approximately 42,000. However, this pass budget can be substantially optimized in future versions, as a large portion of the current sampling is spent on proving unhelpful or redundant lemmas.

In a recent development, notably, these results indicate a shift in the scaling behavior of the prover. While earlier versions exhibited approximately linear improvements in log scale with increasing sampling budget, the current system highlights diminishing returns beyond pass@1024. This suggests that further gains are less dependent on increased sampling and instead require more sophisticated search strategies, such as those introduced by TTRL.

According to recent reports, the lemma-enabled pattern is designed to equip the model with the ability to identify and utilize useful lemmas provided in the input. To support this capability, during reinforcement learning (RL) training, a random subset of one to three formal lemmas is prepended to the problem context, exposing the prover to potentially useful intermediate results that can aid in constructing the final proof. These lemmas are prepared through a two-step pipeline: (1) a general-purpose LLM generates candidate lemmas in natural language; (2) these are then translated into formal statements using our Kimina-Autoformalizer-7b.

Initial observations highlighted that the model had a low tendency to incorporate the provided lemmas. To address this, we introduced a preference-based reward shaping strategy within the RL framework. When a theorem could be proven through multiple trajectories, solutions that successfully leveraged a provided lemma were assigned a higher reward, while those that did not were penalized. This approach proved effective, increasing the lemma utilization rate to a stable 30–40% after training. Importantly, this method not only encouraged lemma usage but also promoted selectivity: the model learned to apply lemmas strategically when they were useful, while ignoring irrelevant ones, demonstrating more efficient and human-like reasoning behavior.

The lemma-enabled pattern allowed the model to incorporate pre-generated lemmas as intermediate steps in constructing proofs. However, we observed that randomly sampling and inserting lemmas was insufficient for solving complex problems requiring highly structured and deeply nested reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search framework—a trainable, agentic approach that systematically organizes, filters, and composes a large set of candidate lemmas to build complete proofs. This framework transitions the process from random exploration to a more strategic, goal-directed search.

As illustrated in Figure 2, we define the search scope of each problem as the problem itself along with its associated candidate lemmas. TTRL Search tracks a lemma utilization score within each search scope to measure how frequently and effectively each lemma contributes to the final proof. At the beginning of each RL training iteration, for each problem (i.e., search scope), we construct K = 10 input variants by prepending different combinations of lemmas. To balance exploration and exploitation, 60% of the inputs are built using the top-ranking lemmas—those with the highest utilization scores—focusing the model on the most promising proof paths. The remaining 40% are formed by including these top lemmas alongside one to four randomly selected additional lemmas, encouraging exploration of novel and potentially useful lemma combinations.

To ensure quality, a filtering mechanism prunes lemmas that consistently fail to contribute meaningfully: any lemma that fails to achieve a utilization score of at least τ=0.10 after 50 insertion attempts is removed from the search pool.

A key feature of TTRL is its recursive search mechanism. The search scope is not limited to the original theorem but is also maintained for each lemma, allowing the framework to recursively decompose the problem into smaller subproblems. A parallel sublemma generation process runs throughout, and whenever a theorem or lemma fails to find a proof after N = 128 attempts, newly introduced candidate sublemmas are generated. This recursive strategy enables test-time scaling of reasoning depth, significantly extending the model’s effective problem-solving capability.

To maintain logical soundness, we address a failure mode wherein incorrectly formalized lemmas could lead to trivial or invalid proofs. In such cases, the model may exploit inconsistencies to construct seemingly valid but unsound solutions. To prevent this, we introduce a negation proving process: for each newly generated lemma, we attempt to prove its logical negation. If the negated statement is provable, it indicates that the original lemma is logically inconsistent and is immediately discarded. This step ensures the reliability and soundness of the overall proof construction process.

A critical limitation of recent advanced theorem proving models is their lack of the ability to correct proofs based on feedback from the proof assistant—capabilities that human consumers routinely leverage. To address this gap, we developed a dedicated framework to integrate error-fixing capabilities into Kimina-Prover.

Recent findings suggest that SFT Data Generation for Error Correction. General-purpose large language models exhibit a low success rate when interpreting Lean’s error messages and proposing valid corrections. To overcome this, we constructed a specialized Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dataset tailored for error correction. This dataset consists of triplets in the form of (incorrect proof, Lean feedback, correct proof). To enrich the supervision signal, we prompted Claude 3.7 sonnet[8] to synthesize step-by-step reasoning chains explaining how the incorrect proof can be transformed into the correct one using the provided feedback. The result is a high-quality dataset that includes not only the initial and corrected proofs but also the intermediate reasoning, facilitating more effective learning.

Batched Failure Replay Strategy. Integrating error correction directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop initially proved ineffective due to the low success rate (~1%) of the SFT model in fixing errors, resulting in sparse rewards and unstable training. To address this, we designed the Batched Failure Replay strategy. Rather than attempting to correct errors immediately during an RL iteration, all failed proof attempts from iteration N are collected. In the subsequent iteration N+1, the training batch is composed of a fixed-size union of these prior failures (e.g., 500 samples) and standard problems from the prompt set (e.g., another 500 samples). This ensures consistent and high-volume exposure to error correction tasks in each training step, enabling the model to gradually learn effective error-handling behaviors in a stable and data-efficient manner.

Recent findings suggest that this training approach led to measurable improvements in the model’s ability to recover from failure. The model advanced from correcting basic syntax errors to resolving complex logical mistakes and, eventually, discovering alternative proof strategies when initial attempts failed. Crucially, this capability improved sample efficiency. As shown in Table 2, we compared different strategies under fixed computational budgets. The 16+16 attempt-and-fix strategy—consisting of 16 initial proof attempts, each followed by one error-fixing attempt—achieved a success rate of 35.6%, outperforming the 32×1 brute-force baseline, which reached 28.8% with 32 independent attempts. Further increasing the sample budget to 32+32 with error correction yielded a success rate of 44.1%. These results demonstrate that enabling the model to correct its own errors is a more efficient use of computational resources than repeated trial-and-error.

In addition to our core TTRL search and Error fixing, we developed several other novel techniques to enhance the model's learning process and problem-solving capabilities.

According to recent reports, prompt Set Curation and Iteration. Effective data curation is critical for reinforcement learning (RL) efficiency. Our initial prompt set of over 300K problems was refined to a competition-focused subset of approximately 90K, with an emphasis on problems from sources such as the olympiads-ref subset of NuminaMath 1.5[9]. During RL, we applied dynamic filtering: problems with consistently high success rates were removed to maintain challenge, while persistently difficult problems were decomposed into simpler subproblems or variations using a general-purpose LLM. The final prompt set combines auto-formalized statements for broad coverage, human-annotated problems for quality, and augmented variations for targeted skill development. The curated prompt set will be open-sourced.

According to recent reports, continuous Pre-training on Lean Data. To address the limited Lean proficiency in most base models, we applied Continuous Pre-training (CPT). A 6-billion-token CPT dataset was constructed from multiple sources: 260M tokens from online platforms such as GitHub, 5.5B tokens of compiler-validated rollout data from our RL pipeline, and additional structured data in state–tactic–state and state–tactic–error formats to enhance diversity. These structured data supplements the base model with additional domain knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that random Proof Cut Data Augmentation. To better utilize high-quality, human-annotated proofs that lack intermediate reasoning steps, we developed the Random Proof Cut technique. This method augments such data using two variations:.

This strategy allows the model to learn how to extend existing lines of reasoning and to fill in logical gaps, effectively integrating human-generated content into the training process.

According to recent reports, non-proof Problem Solving. Many problems are presented in the form of requiring a final answer, which cannot be naturally framed as a traditional proof task. Inspired by the CombiBench[10] evaluation methodology, we introduced a capability for non-proof problem solving to unify answer generation with proof construction. In this setting, the model is given a problem with the final answer field left blank. It performs a two-stage process within a single inference: it first deduces the correct answer and then generates a complete formal proof to justify that answer. This approach ensures the model’s reasoning is explicitly conditioned on reaching the correct solution.

Here we provide some proof cases found by our newest Kimina-prover model. The complete list of solved miniF2F problems is available on GitHub.

In a recent development, the system recursively decomposed the problem into four layers of lemmas using a TTRL search approach, ultimately generating a 520-line formal proof. During this recursive proving process, initially, only one lemma, sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero, remained to be solved. While this conclusion seems straightforward to prove informally, it would still require a lot of steps to prove it rigorously in Lean 4. Our system recursively generated two extra layers of lemmas and obtained a 260-line formal proof for sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero. This proof is valid under Mathlib v4.15.

In the following example, the initial proof timed out because directly applying simp to ((Real.sqrt 3 / 2 : ℂ) + (1 / 2) * Complex.I) ^ 12 resulted in excessive search complexity. Breaking down the proof by step-by-step calculating intermediate powers like $z^3$, then $z^6$, and finally $z^{12}$ significantly reduced the computational burden on the compiler.

If you'd like to cite Kimina-Prover, please feel free to reference our preview paper for now. A full paper is right now in preparation and will be available soon.
