📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

Industry observers note that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

In a recent development, chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.

Recent findings suggest that “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng states in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”.

Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”.

Sources indicate that classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.

In a recent development, the expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active customers are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com right now has but remarked the site is “doing amazingly well.”.

So, while the organization is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.

In a recent development, AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 latest games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.

“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”.

AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng states. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”.

“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”.

In a recent development, chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the manufacturer was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”.

Industry observers note that elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more crucial. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the tech giant has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.

In a recent development, chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng remarked it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that former Nvidia robotics engineer Darrell Dai made a viral post just nine days ago announcing his resignation from Nvidia, which has gathered over 7 million impressions on X alone (Dai also posted to his LinkedIn account). Dai resigned due to what he described as a lack of transparency around CEO Jensen Huang's exit. But now that Huang is back at the helm, Dai has followed up, saying that he "may have moved too quickly," although his resignation has already taken effect.

Welcome back, Jensen. I’m happy to see you return, and happy for my friends and former colleagues at NVIDIA. Looking back, I may have moved too rapidly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning. Thank you for all the kindness and encouragement. Whatever comes next, I want to approach it with a clearer mind and give it the thought it deserves.November 23, 2026.

Dai indicates that although he's open to the possibility of returning to Nvidia, he wants to approach his next decision with "a clearer mind." Huang resigned 11 days ago following reports of two separate affairs, one of which reportedly involved an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Industry observers note that despite reports of belligerent behaviors toward employees, Nvidia retains an exceptional rating on Glassdoor, and many employees rallied around the CEO's return. A petition to reinstate Huang gathered over 150,000 signatures online, including high-profile names like Elon Musk.

It has been revealed that huang publicly admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. In his statement, the Nvidia co-founder apologized to his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang, and his two children, Spencer Huang and Madison Huang, both of whom still work at Nvidia.

Days following the admission, a report from The Fresh York Times accused Huang of having another affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang, citing five anonymous sources within Nvidia. Huang resigned as CEO the following day. Neither Huang nor Powell have commented on the alleged affair.

Dai's last day at Nvidia was November 19, just a few days ago. President Donald Trump stated on Monday that he contacted Nvidia's board, and went as far as to claim he "made the deal," according to CNBC. Following the announcement of Huang's return, Nvidia's stock rose more than 30% upon market open.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In January of this year, Hugging Face's Xet Team deployed a upcoming storage backend, and shortly after shifted ~6% of Hub downloads through the infrastructure. This represented a significant milestone, but it was just the beginning. In 6 months, 500,000 repositories holding 20 PB joined the move to Xet as the Hub outgrows Git LFS and transitions to a storage system that scales with the workloads of AI builders.

Today, more than 1 million people on the Hub are using Xet. In May, it became the default on the Hub for newly introduced owners and organizations. With only a few dozen GitHub problems, forum threads, and Discord messages, this is perhaps the quietest migration of this magnitude.

How? For one, the team came prepared with years of experience building and supporting the content addressed store (CAS) and Rust client that provide the system's foundation. Without these pieces, Git LFS may still be the future on the Hub. However, the unsung heroes of this migration are:.

Sources indicate that together, these components have allowed us to aggressively migrate PBs in the span of days without worrying about the impact to the Hub or the community. They're giving us the peace of mind to move even faster in the coming weeks and months (skip to the end 👇 to see what's coming).

In the early days of planning the migration to Xet, we made a few key design decisions:.

It has been revealed that driven by our commitment to the community, these seemingly straightforward decisions had significant implications. Most importantly, we did not believe users and teams should have to immediately alter their workflow or download a new client to interact with Xet-enabled repositories.

Industry observers note that if you have a Xet-aware client (e.g., hf-xet, the Xet integration with huggingface_hub), uploads and downloads pass through the entire Xet stack. The client either breaks up files into chunks using content defined chunking while uploading, or requests file reconstruction information when downloading. On upload, chunks are passed to CAS and stored in S3. During downloads, CAS provides the chunk ranges the client needs to request from S3 to reconstruct the file locally.

Industry observers note that for older versions of huggingface_hub or huggingface.js, which do not support chunk-based file transfers, you can still download and upload to Xet repos, but these bytes take a different route. When a Xet-backed file is requested from the Hub along the resolve endpoint, the Git LFS Bridge constructs and returns a single presigned URL, mimicking the LFS protocol. The Bridge then does the work of reconstructing the file from the content held in S3 and returns it to the requester.

To see this in action, right click on the image above and open it in a newly introduced tab. The URL redirects from https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/migrating-the-hub-to-xet/bridge.png to one that begins with https://cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co/xet-bridge-us/.... You can also use curl -vL on the same URL to see the redirects in your terminal.

Meanwhile, when a non-Xet-aware client uploads a file, it is sent first to LFS storage then migrated to Xet. This “background migration process,” only briefly mentioned in our docs, powers both the migrations to Xet and upload backward compatibility. It is behind the migration of well over a dozen PBs of models and datasets and is keeping 500,000 repos in sync with Xet storage all without missing a beat.

Every time a file needs to be migrated from LFS to Xet, a webhook is triggered, pushing the event to a distributed queue where it is processed by an orchestrator. The orchestrator:.

These migration workers then pick up the jobs and each pod:.

Sources indicate that in April, we tested this system's limits by reaching out to bartowski and asking if they wanted to test out Xet. With nearly 500 TB across 2,000 repos, bartowski's migration uncovered a few weak links:.

Industry observers note that fixing this three-headed monster meant touching every layer - patching xet-core, resizing CAS, and beefing up the worker node specs. Fortunately, bartowski was game to work with us while every repo made its way to Xet. These same lessons powered the moves of the biggest storage users on the Hub like RichardErkhov (1.7PB and 25,000 repos) and mradermacher (6.1PB and 42,000 repos 🤯).

CAS throughput, meanwhile, has grown by an order of magnitude between the first and latest large-scale migrations:.

When we began replacing LFS, we had two goals in mind:.

Designing with our initial constraints and these goals allowed us to:.

Instead of waiting for all upload paths to become Xet-aware, forcing a hard cut-over, or pushing the community to adopt a specific workflow, we could begin migrating the Hub to Xet immediately with minimal user impact. In short, let teams keep their workflows and organically transition to Xet with infrastructure supporting the long-term goal of a unified storage system.

In January and February, we onboarded power users to provide feedback and pressure-test the infrastructure. To get community feedback, we introduced a waitlist to preview Xet-enabled repositories. Soon after, Xet became the default for new users on the Hub.

We now support some of the largest creators on the Hub (Meta Llama, Google, OpenAI, and Qwen) while the community keeps working uninterrupted.

It has been revealed that starting this month, we're bringing Xet to everyone. Watch for an email providing access to Xet and once you have it, patch to the latest huggingface_hub (pip install -U huggingface_hub) to unlock faster transfers right away. This will also mean:.

In a recent development, if you upload or download from the Hub using your browser or use Git, that's fine. Chunk-based support for both is coming soon. In the meantime use whichever workflow you already have; no restrictions.

According to recent reports, next up: open-sourcing the Xet protocol and the entire infrastructure stack. The future of storing and moving bytes that scale to AI workloads is on the Hub, and we're aiming to bring it to everyone.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇, open a discussion on the Xet team page.

Perhaps a dumb question: Xet is supposed to not only drive some speed ups but also provide a significant storage advantage in that only the diffs of a given object need to be uploaded/stored right?

Not a dumb question at all. The Hub reports storage based on the logical size of each new object; what you're seeing is expected.

For the use-case that you're describing, Xet still provides faster file transfers as there is less to push and pull, so changes finish faster and uses less bandwidth/compute.

This enables and strengthens our commitment to provide free public storage to the open source community. Of course, we're always evaluating ways to surface this transparently and support the community, so let me know if any of this is confusing.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

It has been revealed that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

It has been revealed that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two key parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

It has been revealed that for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/consumers.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Sources indicate that swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a upcoming optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Recent findings suggest that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

Industry observers note that this becomes particularly notable when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document notable endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model?
  • According to recent reports, we introduce a new open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!).
  • This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model? Turns out, a state-of-the-art decoder language model that beats Llama 3.2 1B and SmolLM2!

According to recent reports, we introduce a new open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!). We then apply the exact same recipe to decoder-only models. For the first time, we have two state-of-the-art models trained in the same setup but with two different training objectives: masked language modeling (MLM), and causal language modeling (CLM).

This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes. Ettin enables true apples-to-apples comparisons between architectures and delivers state-of-the-art performance for open-data models in both categories. We then further explore whether it is possible to get a competitive encoder starting from the decoder and vice-versa.

If you are interested in trying out the models, some boilerplates are available at the end of this blogpost!

In a recent development, the LLM community has largely converged on decoder-only models like GPT, Llama, and Qwen. Their generative capabilities are impressive, but this focus is detracting attention from other categories, such as encoder-only models like BERT.

However, encoder BERT-like models remain the workhorses of production systems for classification, retrieval, and embedding tasks. They're faster, more memory-efficient, and often more accurate for discriminative tasks. The key difference lies in their attention patterns:.

According to recent reports, while decoder models have seen rapid innovation, encoder model development had stagnated – until recently, with efforts like ModernBERT modernizing them. But which architecture is better? Previous comparisons between encoders and decoders used different datasets, architectures, and training recipes, so it was hard to tell.

Industry observers note that named after the two-headed Norse giant, Ettin provides a controlled comparison by training with both architectures on identical data, identical model shapes, and identical training recipes. They only differ in attention patterns and training objectives!

According to recent reports, we build on the ModernBERT recipe, which borrowed modern techniques from decoder-only models and brought them to encoder training. This provides a strong base for training both architectures.

We train six different sizes, ranging from 17M to 1B parameters. This allows us to test the effects of scale, and provides a wide variety of models for you to use! No matter if you need a blazing fast on-device model or a powerful but slower model, we got you covered!

We use a comprehensive three-phase training approach to maximize performance:.

Phase 1 - Pre-training (1.7T tokens): We start with a diverse mixture of high-quality data sources, training on shorter contexts (1024 tokens) to establish strong foundational knowledge.

Phase 2 - Context Extension (250B tokens): We increase context length to 8K tokens using higher-quality filtered data, allowing models to understand longer documents and more complex relationships.

Phase 3 - Decay (100B tokens): We finish with premium data sources including scientific papers, textbooks, and curated content while gradually reducing the learning rate.

Our encoder models gain all the benefits of ModernBERT's speed, allowing them to be significantly faster than the previous generations of encoders.

Unlike ModernBERT, all our training data is public and reproducible:.

You can continue to train these models on new data or propose a new recipe to further improve results!

Our encoder models outperform ModernBERT across all tasks and model sizes, while using completely open training data. Since we provide a large range of sizes, you can now use ModernBERT-style models in smaller sizes (great for on-device or for fast-inference), or power up with a 1B-sized encoder that crushes the competition.

Applying the same recipe to decoder models yields equally impressive results, with our models outperforming or matching established baselines such as Llama 3.2 and SmolLM2:.

According to recent reports, the gains are particularly strong on knowledge-intensive tasks like SciQ, reflecting the benefits of our high-quality training data mixture. These results demonstrate that our training recipe creates genuinely strong models in both architectural paradigms.

Sources indicate that for the first time, we can fairly compare encoder and decoder architectures trained with identical data and recipes. The results reveal fundamental architectural advantages that persist even when all other factors are controlled:.

The results show clear patterns:.

Recent findings suggest that encoders dominate classification and retrieval: On MNLI classification, even a 150M encoder (89.2) outperforms a 400M decoder (88.2). For retrieval tasks, the gap is smaller but still noticeable - especially when decoders are not trained with MNTP.

Decoders excel at generation: On generative tasks, decoders maintain consistent advantages, with the performance gap actually widening at larger model sizes.

Size doesn't always matter: A 400M encoder beats a 1B decoder on classification tasks, while a 400M decoder beats a 1B encoder on generation tasks.

Due to the lack of new encoder models, works like LLM2Vec have proposed to continue pre-training decoders with MLM. We can now test the effectiveness of this strategy!

We switched the objective and continued to train our models with the opposite objective for 50B additional tokens. This is what we found:.

This suggests the architecture choice matters fundamentally, not just the training objective.

With identical training data, we can study how different objectives affect learning. For example, analyzing gender bias using the WinoGender benchmark reveals:.

This opens doors for systematic studies of how training objectives influence model behavior beyond just accuracy metrics.

For text generation tasks, use decoder models:.

While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” consumers on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

Five Big Improvements to Gradio MCP Servers

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications.
  • To that end, here are some of the substantial improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.
  • If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting substantial on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the substantial improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

While many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

Sources indicate that gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and key security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

According to recent reports, depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

As an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide shows you how.

If you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

OpenAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

Industry observers note that A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your users. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

In a recent development, to make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

Gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

Want us to add a latest MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.
  • It has been revealed that the Nest app has been on life support for years now.
  • Realistically, even long-time Nest owners have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

It has been revealed that the Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest owners have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

According to recent reports, having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a massive fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That remarked, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

According to recent reports, google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Industry observers note that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Recent findings suggest that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

According to recent reports, the Free initiative is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Recent findings suggest that lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Recent findings suggest that base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every initiative, Free included.

Recent findings suggest that base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Sources indicate that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

It has been revealed that bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

According to recent reports, bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web prepares run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

In a recent development, v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

Recent findings suggest that v0's Free blueprint gives new consumers $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Sources indicate that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

It has been revealed that collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

It has been revealed that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human customers.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

It has been revealed that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Industry News: Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations).
  • Forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information.
  • Beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations). However, we believe that more valuable AI, and ultimately AGI, will be distinguished by its ability to use this past to forecast interesting aspects of the future, rather than merely reciting old facts.

Forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information. Evaluating models on their ability to predict future outcomes, whether in science, economics, geopolitics, or technology tests the kind of intelligence that creates real-world value.

Beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks. Traditional benchmarks that measure accuracy on fixed test sets are inevitably affected by possible data contamination, and without access to the full reproducible training pipeline of a model, it's hard to trust the results. The most serious evaluation efforts now keep their test sets completely private, creating a frustrating arms race between evaluators and potential "gaming the leaderboard" mechanics (Singh et al., 2025).

Forecasting makes contamination impossible by design, as you can't train on data that doesn't yet exist! This creates a level playing field where success depends on reasoning capability rather than memorization.

Perhaps most importantly, predictions about the future are inherently verifiable. We can wait and see who was right, creating an objective, time-stamped measure of model performance.

Recent findings suggest that we therefore propose evaluating agents on their ability to predict future events (Ye et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025). FutureBench draws from real-world prediction markets and emerging news to create interesting prediction tasks grounded in actual future outcomes. We collect events from platforms and live news coverages and manifold markets, filtering them to focus on emerging events worth predicting. Using an agent-based approach, we curate scenarios that require genuine reasoning rather than simple pattern matching. Think geopolitical developments, market movements, or technology adoption trends - events where informed analysis actually matters.

It has been revealed that this is the obvious question, and it's at the heart of what makes this benchmark interesting! We believe the answer cannot be a simple “yes” or a “no”, as it mostly depends on the actual questions; there are always important caveats to consider. Humans constantly use their ability to weigh current information to predict future events. Aren't most career moves, relationship choices, or even business strategies essentially bets on future outcomes?

In a recent development, some predictions involve irreducible uncertainty (Will it rain on December 17th, 2027 at noon?), but many don't. When a skilled analyst predicts a organization's quarterly earnings or a policy expert forecasts election outcomes, they're using available information to make informed decisions. This is precisely what we're asking AI agents to do with FutureBench! The task isn't to get agents to fortune-tell, but rather to synthesize information and reason under stronger uncertainty than most other benchmarks.

The agent's prediction quality directly reflects its ability to search relevant information, synthesize complex data, and reason about cause-and-effect relationships. These are precisely the capabilities we want to measure in real-world applications.

Tools like DeepResearch are already used for market analysis and strategic planning. The quality of information collection strongly correlates with decision-making effectiveness. FutureBench is inspired by this evaluation process and tries to compute agents’ quality with objective, verifiable outcomes.

Industry observers note that building a benchmark that tests real prediction capabilities requires a steady stream of meaningful questions. We've developed two complementary approaches that capture different types of future events:.

Our first approach uses AI to mine current events for prediction opportunities. We deploy a smolagents-based agent to scrape a few major news websites, analyze front-page articles, and generate prediction questions about their likely outcomes. The agent reads through and identifies interesting articles and formulates specific, time-bound questions from their content, for example "Will the Federal Reserve cut interest rates by at least 0.25% by July 1st, 2025?".

We guide this process with carefully crafted prompts that specify what makes a good prediction question—events that are meaningful, verifiable, and uncertain extraction time.

Industry observers note that the agent typically generates 5 questions per scraping session, with a time horizon of a single week, meaning that we assume we’ll know the answer to the question after seven days. This gives us a natural pipeline of fresh evaluation material tied to real-world events.

Our second source draws from Polymarket. These questions come from a prediction market platform where real participants make forecasts about future events. We at the moment ingest around 8 questions per week.

However, the raw data needs filtering. We apply strong filtering to remove general questions regarding temperature and some questions regarding the stock and crypto markets, which would otherwise be too numerous for practical use in our benchmark. In addition to this, polymarket questions have less constraints regarding the final “realization” time, the actual outcome of the event could be available only next month or by the end of the year. These are still very relevant questions, but the data collection of the outcome is more sparse.

Here's an example of what comes out of our question generation pipeline:.

The next question is, what does this type of benchmark allow us to measure? The framework operates on three distinct levels, allowing us to isolate exactly what we're measuring:.

It has been revealed that level 1: Framework Comparison Keep the underlying LLMs and tools constant while varying frameworks. How does a LangChain-based agent compare to one built with CrewAI when both use GPT-4 and the same search tools? This isolates the impact of different agentic frameworks.

According to recent reports, level 2: Tool Performance Fix the LLM and framework while comparing different implementations. Which search tool (for example Tavily, Google, Bing) leads to better predictions than other search engines, holding everything else constant? This reveals which tools actually provide value. How much value do tools bring in general with respect to models without tools?

According to recent reports, level 3: Model Capabilities Hold the framework and tools constant while testing different LLMs. Given access to the same set of tools, does DeepSeek-V3 use them as effectively as GPT-4? This measures pure reasoning ability. This systematic approach lets us understand exactly where performance gains and losses occur in the agent pipeline.

The benchmark also serves as a robust test of instruction following. Agents must respect specific formatting requirements and generate actions that can be correctly parsed and executed. In practice, this often reveals where smaller language models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that 🚀 Try it yourself! Explore the live leaderboard: FutureBench Interactive Leaderboard.

Recent findings suggest that we use SmolAgents as a baseline agent framework for all the questions. We also compute performance on the base models. For the prediction task itself, the agents get access to a focused toolkit:.

This intentionally lean setup forces agents to be strategic about information gathering while still providing the tools needed for informed predictions.

We compare different models using smolagents as a baseline (you can find the leaderboard on our HF Space). We also run the standard language models without internet access to estimate a general prior. As expected, we see agentic models performing better than simple language models; stronger models show more stable prediction quality. Overall we also find interesting patterns in how different models try to approach a question:.

Running this benchmark has revealed insights into how different models approach information gathering. One striking difference is with respect to scraping. GPT-4.1 appears to rely more on search results. Claude3.7 and 4 explore the web space in more detail and tend to use web scraping more frequently; this thorough approach also means collecting many more input tokens during the research process, thus increasing the cost.

Models show interesting approaches to making predictions, for example, to answer the question "Will annual inflation increase by 2.6 or more in June?":.

The DeepSeekV3 agent analyzed June 2025 inflation prospects by searching recent CPI data (finding current inflation at 2.4-2.8%), considered tariff impacts as upward pressure, and concluded inflation would exceed the 2.6% threshold.

Claude3.7 analyzed June 2025 inflation through comprehensive research (11 searches vs DeepSeekV3's 3), systematically gathering May 2025 CPI data (2.4% year-over-year), identifying decelerating monthly trends (0.2%→0.1%), weighing tariff pressures against Fed restrictive policy, calculating precise 0.2% gap needed, and concluded recent deceleration made reaching 2.6% threshold unlikely, answering "No.".

GPT4.1 analyzed June 2025 inflation through targeted searches for market consensus and forecasts, identified May 2025 CPI at 2.4% (below 2.5% expectations), noted weak 0.1% monthly increases, found no forecaster predictions of 2.6%+ for June, and concluded the jump from 2.4% to 2.6% was unlikely given recent below-expectation trends.

Interestingly, Claude was the only model that tried to access the Bureau of Labor Statistics website to scrape it directly, which failed because it is a .gov website and we do not allow this type of action.

The models exhibit distinct reasoning patterns in their outputs. GPT's analysis focused on consensus forecasts as the key signal for future events rather than extrapolating from current data, while Claude's approach exhibited rigorous analytical structure with its systematic pro/con framework and quantitative gap analysis, and DeepSeekV3's output displayed explicit acknowledgment of data limitations and systematic methodology adjustments when initial approaches encountered constraints.

These behavioral differences reveal interesting patterns in how different models approach information gathering. The variations in web usage and token consumption suggest that models have distinct strategies for tackling prediction tasks, which FutureBench can help us measure and understand.

Industry observers note that one challenge is that evaluation can be expensive due to the large number of input tokens. For example, Claude tends to visit web pages frequently, thus accumulating many input tokens. In a multi-turn loop, this can make the number of input tokens skyrocket very swiftly. This increases the cost of any subsequent generation, even though most tokens are eventually cached.

Sources indicate that futureBench is an evolving benchmark, as we discover new findings and better patterns, we’ll keep incorporating them. We would love feedback from the community to understand how to better source questions, which experiments to run and which data is the most interesting to analyze.

According to recent reports, singh, S., Nan, Y., Wang, A., D'souza, D., Kapoor, S., Ustun, A., Koyejo, S., Deng, Y., Longpre, S., Smith, N., Ermiş, B.H., Fadaee, M., & Hooker, S. (2025). The Leaderboard Illusion. ArXiv, abs/2504.20879.

According to recent reports, karger, E., Bastani, H., Yueh-Han, C., Jacobs, Z., Halawi, D., Zhang, F., & Tetlock, P.E. (2025). ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities. ICLR.

Japan puts chipmaking labs inside trucks with mobileFab

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple nations worldwide have chip-making programs in their respective universities, a discipline that is seeing increasing demand by the day.
  • Each truck-mounted mobileFab container contains three machines: a photoresist coater, a maskless lithography machine, and a photoresist developer.
  • The three machines going into trucks are part of the larger Minimal Fab laboratories in place in some Japanese colleges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple nations worldwide have chip-making programs in their respective universities, a discipline that is seeing increasing demand by the day. Japan is one such nation, and it currently has a program in which students can design circuits to wire chip wafers with miniaturized lithography stations. That gear is now going on wheels to schools and companies thanks to mobileFab trucks.

Each truck-mounted mobileFab container contains three machines: a photoresist coater, a maskless lithography machine, and a photoresist developer. Students take pre-etched wafers made by Japan's NIAIST (Institute for Advanced Industrial Science and Technology) and go through the necessary steps to wire the transistors therein together and produce a finalized chip core. The procedures are analogous to getting a breadboard with some pre-mounted, unconnected components and turning that into a product.

The three machines going into trucks are part of the larger Minimal Fab laboratories in place in some Japanese colleges. They're going on the move so that other schools and companies can train students/employees in the art of chipmaking. For now, the 12.5-mm wafers come from the NIAIST, but they can come from other foundries. Each machine is roughly 30 cm wide, and the machines use localized cleaning and sealed between-machine transportation so as not to have to rely on large-scale cleanrooms.

Recent findings suggest that according to the press release by the Minimal Fab Promotion Organization, this system is not only meant for democratizing access to chip manufacturing education. The machines also allow for rapid prototyping and iteration of chip designs, and facilitate small-scale manufacturing — all with modest capital investment.

According to recent reports, the "why" of this initiative is fairly predictable: the program's organizers predict that semiconductor fab engineers will be in high demand over the next 10 years, and there aren't even enough teachers going around, making systematic education difficult. Additionally, the division of labor in semiconductor fabs means that many engineers don't participate in all stages of the chip-making process, nor do they have opportunities to operate chip-making equipment themselves. The mobileFab will be on display at the SEMICON Japan 2026 conference in December.

Consilium: When Multiple LLMs Collaborate

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time.
  • The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had concerns as the timeout could not be adjusted).
  • This wasn't my original hackathon idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time. That's exactly what Consilium, the multi-LLM platform I built during the Gradio Agents & MCP Hackathon, does. It lets AI models discuss complex questions and reach consensus through structured debate.

The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had concerns as the timeout could not be adjusted). The core idea was always about LLMs reaching consensus through discussion; that's where the name Consilium came from. Later, other decision modes like majority voting and ranked choice were added to make the collaboration more sophisticated.

This wasn't my original hackathon idea. I initially wanted to build a simple MCP server to talk to my projects in RevenueCat. But I reconsidered when I realized a multi-LLM platform where these models discuss questions and return well-reasoned answers would be far more compelling.

The timing turned out to be perfect. Shortly after the hackathon, Microsoft published their AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which is essentially an AI doctor panel with different roles like "Dr. Challenger Agent" that iteratively diagnose patients. In their setup with OpenAI o3, they correctly solved 85.5% of medical diagnosis benchmark cases, while practicing physicians achieved only 20% accuracy. This validates exactly what Consilium demonstrates: multiple AI perspectives collaborating can dramatically outperform individual analysis.

After settling on the concept, I needed something that worked as both an MCP server and an engaging Hugging Face space demo. Initially I considered using the standard Gradio Chat component, but I wanted my submission to stand out. The idea was to seat LLMs around a table in a boardroom with speech bubbles, which should capture the collaborative discussion while also making it visually engaging. As I did not manage to style a standard table nicely so it was actually recognized as a table, I went for a poker-style roundtable. This approach also let me submit to two hackathon tracks by building a custom Gradio component and MCP server.

The custom Gradio component became the heart of the submission; the poker-style roundtable where participants sit and display speech bubbles showing their responses, thinking status, and research activities immediately caught the eye of anyone visiting the space. The component development was remarkably smooth thanks to Gradio's excellent developer experience, though I did encounter one documentation gap around PyPI publishing that led to my first contribution to the Gradio project.

The visual design proved robust throughout the hackathon; after the initial implementation, only features like user-defined avatars and center table text were added, while the core interaction model remained unchanged.

If you are interested in creating your own custom Gradio component you should take a look at Custom Components in 5 minutes and yes the title does not lie; it literally only takes 5 minutes for the basic setup.

It has been revealed that the visual roundtable maintains state through a session-based dictionary system where each user gets isolated state storage via user_sessions[session_id]. The core state object tracks participants, messages, currentSpeaker, thinking, and showBubbles arrays that are updated through update_visual_state() callbacks. When models are thinking, speaking, or research is being executed, the engine pushes incremental state updates to the frontend by appending to the messages array and toggling speaker/thinking states, creating the real-time visual flow without complex state machines - just direct JSON state mutations synchronized between backend processing and frontend rendering.

While implementing, I realized there was no real discussion happening between the LLMs because they lacked clear roles. They received the full context of ongoing discussions but didn't know how to engage meaningfully. I introduced distinct roles to create productive debate dynamics, which, after a few tweaks, ended up being like this:.

Recent findings suggest that this solved the discussion problem but raised a new question: how to determine consensus or identify the strongest argument? I implemented a lead analyst system where users select one LLM to synthesize the final result and evaluate whether consensus was reached.

Recent findings suggest that I also wanted owners to control communication structure. Beyond the default full-context sharing, I added two alternative modes:.

Finally, discussions need endpoints. I implemented configurable rounds (1-5), with testing showing that more rounds increase the likelihood of reaching consensus (though at higher computational cost).

Industry observers note that the current model selection includes Mistral Large, DeepSeek-R1, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B, and QwQ-32B. While notable models like Claude Sonnet and OpenAI's o3 are absent, this reflected hackathon credit availability and sponsor award considerations rather than technical limitations.

It has been revealed that for models supporting function calling, I integrated a dedicated research agent that appears as another roundtable participant. Rather than giving models direct web access, this agent approach provides visual clarity about external resource availability and ensures consistent access across all function-calling models.

The research agent accesses five sources: Web Search, Wikipedia, arXiv, GitHub, and SEC EDGAR. I built these tools on an extensible base class architecture for future expansion while focusing on freely embeddable resources.

Since research operations can be time-intensive, the speech bubbles display progress indicators and time estimates to maintain user engagement during longer research tasks.

It has been revealed that after the hackathon, Deborah Dahl introduced me to the Open Floor Protocol, which aligns perfectly with the roundtable approach. This protocol provides standardized JSON message formatting for cross-platform agent communication. Its key differentiator from other agent-to-agent protocols is that all agents maintain constant conversation awareness exactly like sitting at the same table. Another feature I have not seen with other protocols is that the floor manager can dynamically invite and remove agents from the floor and agents.

The protocol's interaction patterns map directly to Consilium's architecture:.

I'm presently integrating Open Floor Protocol support to allow consumers to add any OFP-compliant agents to their roundtable discussions. You can follow this development at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/azettl/consilium_ofp.

The hackathon introduced me to multi-agent debate research I hadn't previously encountered, including foundational studies like Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate. The community experience was remarkable; all participants actively supported each other through Discord feedback and collaboration. Seeing my roundtable component integrated into another hackathon project was one of my highlights working on Consilium.

I will continue to work on Consilium and with expanded model selection, Open Floor Protocol integration, and configurable agent roles, the platform could support virtually any multi-agent debate scenario imaginable.

Building Consilium reinforced my conviction that AI's future lies not just in more powerful individual models but in systems enabling effective AI collaboration. As specialized smaller language models become more efficient and resource-friendly, I believe roundtables of task-specific SLMs with dedicated research agents may provide compelling alternatives to general-purpose large language models for many use cases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that folding phones are entering a upcoming chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most vital questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Recent findings suggest that samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:.

It has been revealed that starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

Industry observers note that with each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most crucial priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

According to recent reports, when it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That noted, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

According to recent reports, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

Industry observers note that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

It has been revealed that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

According to recent reports, galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

In a recent development, if you are moving into a upcoming Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

#172221. Shared CXL memory comes with a software tax — a real four-server test found locks cost 3–5 µs each
