📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Shared CXL memory comes with a software tax — a real four-server test found locks cost 3–5 µs each

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware.
  • Locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it.
  • The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.

Locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.

The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”.

This means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.

According to recent reports, the result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.

Those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a latest home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description indicates cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”.

SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, indicated a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.

Sources indicate that the need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research said at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face shows KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, showed that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.

That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody mentioned. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.

It doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.

It has been revealed that limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du stated, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.

In a recent development, micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.

Micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.

In a recent development, working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole said; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or announced memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such big data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.

In a recent development, A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.

It has been revealed that CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the company’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing rapidly.

It has been revealed that on paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

According to a newly introduced report, Samsung’s next “Galaxy Watch 10” won’t be releasing in 2027 with the company moving to a bi-yearly release schedule for its smartwatches.

ETNews reports that Samsung will not have a fresh Galaxy Watch model releasing in 2027, a series that would have likely been called “Galaxy Watch 10.” The reason, the report suggests, is that Samsung is “undertaking a structural overhaul to strengthen profitability” (translated) following two quarters in a row of losses in its mobile division.

Samsung has released a latest Galaxy Watch every year since 2018, with 2021’s Galaxy Watch 4 marking the switch to Wear OS.

Industry observers note that the new schedule will apparently see new Galaxy Watch releases every other year, pushing the next release into 2028. The report goes on to mention that Galaxy Watch is part of a “mature phase” of the smartwatch market, and that Galaxy Watch 9 sales “fell short of expectations” likely due in part to its higher price point.

Apparently, Samsung looks latest Galaxy Watch software updates next year as well as “enhancement of healthcare features.” The Galaxy Fit 4 fitness tracker is also expected in 2027, with Dealabs reporting that the tracker will be priced at €79.90 in Europe, a slight price hike over the previous release.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

According to recent reports, this guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Sources indicate that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

It has been revealed that • Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

Sources indicate that • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

Recent findings suggest that • Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it states it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: the page indicates different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your initiative. It indicates to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

It has been revealed that strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and notes other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The firm’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

In a recent development, copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it notes it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, notes very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Industry observers note that turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Industry observers note that strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Industry observers note that sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page indicates false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

Industry observers note that the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Industry observers note that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

Industry observers note that • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

Sources indicate that • Moving targets. Newly introduced models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

It has been revealed that openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

Recent findings suggest that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as upcoming models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

Industry observers note that • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

It has been revealed that because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

Industry observers note that • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

Industry observers note that • Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

According to recent reports, they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

It has been revealed that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

Arc Virtual Cell Challenge: A Primer

📅 18 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge.
  • Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.
  • Industry observers note that doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge. Participants are required to train a model capable of predicting the effect of silencing a gene in a (partially) unseen cell type, a task they term context generalization. For ML engineers with little to no biology background, the jargon and required context can seem quite daunting. To encourage participation, we recapitulate the challenge in a form better suited to engineers from other disciplines.

Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.

Industry observers note that doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone. What if we could test thousands of drug candidates without ever touching a petri dish? This is the goal of the virtual cell challenge — a model (most likely a neural network) that can simulate exactly what happens to a cell when we change some parameter. Given that tightening your feedback loop is often the best way to speed up progress, a model capable of doing this accurately would have significant impact.

Industry observers note that to train this neural network, we will need data. For the challenge, Arc has curated a dataset of ~300k single-cell RNA sequencing profiles. It may be worthwhile to revisit the Central Dogma before continuing. This essay will build off of this to provide the ~minimum biology knowledge you'll need for the challenge.

According to recent reports, the training set consists of a sparse matrix and some associated metadata. More specifically, we have 220k cells, and for each cell we have a transcriptome. This transcriptome is a sparse row vector, where each entry is the raw count of RNA molecules (transcripts) that the corresponding gene (our column) encodes for. Of the 220k cells, ~38k are unperturbed, meaning no gene has been silenced using CRISPR. These control cells are crucial as we will see shortly.

To understand the dataset more concretely, let's select a gene, TMSB4X (the most frequently silenced gene in the dataset) and compare the number of RNA molecules detected for a control cell and a perturbed cell.

We can see that the cell with TMSB4X silenced has a greatly reduced number of transcripts compared with the control cells.

The astute among you may be wondering why you don't just measure the count of the RNA molecules before and after silencing the gene — why do we need the control cells at all? Unfortunately, reading the transcriptome destroys the cell, which is a problem reminiscent of the observer effect.

Industry observers note that this inability to measure the cell state before and after introduces many complications, as we are forced to use a population of basal (a.k.a control, unperturbed) cells as a reference point. The control cells and perturbed cells are not entirely homogeneous even prior to the perturbation. This means that we have to now separate out our true signal, the perturbation, from noise induced by the heterogeneity.

More formally, we can model observed gene expression in perturbed cells as:.

X^p∼T^p(Dbasal)+H(Dbasal)+ε,ε∼Pε \hat{X}_p \sim \hat{T}_p(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + H(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim P_\varepsilon X^p​∼T^p​(Dbasal​)+H(Dbasal​)+ε,ε∼Pε​.

Prior to the Virtual Cell Challenge, Arc released STATE, their own attempt to solve the challenge using a pair of transformer based models. This serves as a strong baseline for participants to start with, so we will explore it in detail.

In a recent development, STATE consists of two models, the State Transition Model (ST) and the State Embedding Model (SE). SE is designed to produce rich semantic embeddings of cells in an effort to improve cross cell type generalization. ST is the "cell simulator", that takes in either a transcriptome of a control cell, or an embedding of a cell produced by SE, along with a one hot encoded vector representing the perturbation of interest, and outputs the perturbed transcriptome.

The State Transition Model is a relatively simple transformer with a Llama backbone that operates upon the following:.

In a recent development, using a covariate matched set of control cells with paired target cells should assist the model in discerning the actual effect of our intended perturbation. Both the control set tensor and the perturbation tensor are fed through independent encoders, which are simply 4 layer MLPs with GELU activations. If working directly in gene expression space (i.e producing a full transcriptome), they pass the output through a learned decoder.

According to recent reports, ST is trained using Maximum Mean Discrepancy. Put simply, the model learns to minimize the difference between the two probability distributions.

The State Embedding Model is a BERT-like autoencoder. To understand this more deeply, first we have to take a little detour for some more biological grounding.

Sources indicate that A gene consists of exons (protein coding sections) and introns (non-protein coding sections). DNA is first transcribed into pre-mRNA, as shown above. The cell then performs Alternative Splicing. This is basically "pick and choose exons", cut out all introns. You can think of the gene as an IKEA manual for making a table. One could also construct a 3 legged table, perhaps an odd bookshelf with some effort, by leaving out some parts. These different objects are analogous to protein isoforms, proteins coded for by the same gene.

Sources indicate that with this basic understanding, we can move on to how the SE model works. Remember, our core goal for SE is to create meaningful cell embeddings. To do this, we must first create meaningful gene embeddings.

To produce a single gene embedding, we first obtain the amino acid sequence (e.g SDKPDMAEI\texttt{SDKPDMAEI}SDKPDMAEI... for TMSB4X) of all the different protein isoforms encoded for by the gene in question. We then feed these sequences to ESM2, a 15B parameter Protein Language Model from FAIR. ESM produces an embedding per amino acid, and we mean pool them together to obtain a "transcript" (a.k.a protein isoform) embedding.

Industry observers note that now we have all of these protein isoform embeddings, we then just mean pool those to get the gene embedding. Next, we project these gene embeddings to our model dimension using a learned encoder as follows:.

g~j=SiLU(LayerNorm(gjWg+bg)) \tilde{g}_j = \text{SiLU}(\text{LayerNorm}(g_j \mathbf{W}_g + \mathbf{b}_g)) g~​j​=SiLU(LayerNorm(gj​Wg​+bg​)).

Recent findings suggest that we've now obtained a gene embedding, but what we really want is a cell embedding. To do this, Arc represents each cell as the top 2048 genes ranked by log fold expression level.

We then construct a "cell sentence" from our 2048 gene embeddings as follows: c~(i)=[zcls,g~1(i),g~2(i),…,g~L(i),zds]∈R(L+2)×h \tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(i)} = \left[\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_1^{(i)}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_2^{(i)}, \ldots, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_L^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}_{\text{ds}}\right] \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+2) \times h} c~(i)=[zcls​,g~​1(i)​,g~​2(i)​,…,g~​L(i)​,zds​]∈R(L+2)×h.

Sources indicate that we add a [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token and [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token to our sentence. The [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token ends up being used as our "cell embedding" (very BERT-like) and the [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token is used to "disentangle dataset-specific effects". Although the genes are sorted by log fold expression level, Arc further enforces the magnitude of each genes expression by incorporating the transcriptome in a fashion analogous to positional embeddings. Through an odd "soft binning" algorithm and 2 MLPs, they create some "expression encodings" which they then add to each gene embedding. This should modulate the magnitude of each gene embedding by how intensely it is expressed in the transcriptome.

Industry observers note that to train the model, they mask 1280 genes per cell, and the model is tasked with predicting them. The 1280 genes are selected such that they have a wide range of expression intensities. For the graphically inclined, the below demonstrates the construction of the cell sentence.

It has been revealed that understanding how your submission will be evaluated is key to success. The 3 evaluation metrics chosen by Arc are Perturbation Discrimination, Differential Expression and Mean Average Error. Given that Mean Average Error is simple and exactly as it sounds, we will omit it from our analysis.

Perturbation Discrimination intends to evaluate how well your model can uncover relative differences between perturbations. To do this, we compute the Manhattan distances for all the measured perturbed transcriptomes in the test set (the ground truth we are trying to predict, yty_tyt​ and all other perturbed transcriptomes, ypny_p^nypn​) to our predicted transcriptome y^t\hat{y}_ty^​t​. We then rank where the ground truth lands with respect to all transcriptomes as follows:.

According to recent reports, rt=∑p≠t1{d(y^t,yp) After, we normalize by the total number of transcriptomes: PDisct=rtT \text{PDisc}_t = \frac{r_t}{T} PDisct​=Trt​​ Where 000 would be a perfect match. The overall score for your predictions is the mean of all $$\text{PDisc}_t$$. This is then normalized to: PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc \text{PDiscNorm} = 1 - 2\text{PDisc} PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc We multiply by 2 as for a random prediction, ~half of the results would be closer and half would be further away. Differential Expression intends to evaluate what fraction of the truly affected genes did you correctly identify as significantly affected. Firstly, for each gene compute a ppp-value using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with tie correction. We do this for both our predicted perturbation distribution and the ground truth perturbation distribution. Next, we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, basically some stats to modulate the ppp-values, as with 20,00020,00020,000 genes and a ppp-value threshold of 0.050.050.05, you'd expect 1,0001,0001,000 false positives. We denote our set of predicted differentially expressed genes Gp,predG_{p,pred}Gp,pred​, and the ground truth set of differentially expressed genes Gp,trueG_{p,true}Gp,true​. If the size of our set is less than the ground truth set size, take the intersection of the sets, and divide by the true number of differentially expressed genes as follows: DEp=Gp,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{G_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​Gp,pred​∩Gp,true​​ If the size of our set is greater than the ground truth set size, select the subset we predict are most differentially expressed (our "most confident" predictions, denoted G~p,pred\tilde{G}_{p,pred}G~p,pred​), take the intersection with the ground truth set, and then divide by the true number. DEp=G~p,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{\tilde{G}_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​G~p,pred​∩Gp,true​​ Do this for all predicted perturbations and take the mean to obtain the final score.   • Lots of people will be picking up smart rings this year as many models go on sale for Black Friday, but one special RingConn smart ring might make you forget about all that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A special-edition RingConn Gen 3 is The One Ring to rule them all, and you can preorder it now.

Lots of people will be picking up smart rings this year as many models go on sale for Black Friday, but one special RingConn smart ring might make you forget about all that. RingConn’s Gen 3 ring has been transformed into The One Ring, which is up for preorder right now for $399 and ships starting December 8.

The limited-edition gold ring features the legendary Black Speech inscription along the outside, which, thankfully, you won’t need to run through a fire to see. If you preorder now, you’ll receive a sizing kit in the first week of December so you can ensure The One Ring fits properly on your finger. Unfortunately, this one doesn’t auto-size to your hand the way it does in the lore.

Industry observers note that ringConn highlights that none of The One Ring’s features require a subscription, which is the case with any of the rings in the manufacturer’s lineup. The One Ring, like RingConn Gen 3, features a haptic vibration motor inside to alert you of notifications on your phone, something most smart rings don’t even try to do.

It’s also got all the great vascular health, sleep health, women’s health, heart health, and stress & recovery features of RingConn Gen 3, too. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these upcoming Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

Sources indicate that “Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a substantial part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for notable apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

AI builders want a choice of the latest large language models (LLM) architectures and specialized variants for use in AI agents and other apps, but handling all the diversity can slow testing and deployment pipelines. NIM now provides a single docker container for deploying a broad range of LLMs supported by leading inference frameworks from NVIDIA and the community including NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and SGLang. 📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes.
  • In this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x).
  • Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that loRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes. When it comes to image generation, they can empower the models with different styles, different characters, and much more. Sometimes, they can also be leveraged to reduce inference latency. Hence, their importance is paramount, particularly when it comes to customizing and fine-tuning models.

In this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x). It has over 30k adapters trained with it (as reported on the Hugging Face Hub platform). Therefore, its importance to the community is significant.

Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.

If you cannot wait to get started with the code, please check out the accompanying code repository.

When serving LoRAs, it is common to hotswap (swap in and swap out different LoRAs) them. A LoRA changes the base model architecture. Additionally, LoRAs can be different from one another – each one of them could have varying ranks and different layers they target for adaptation. To account for these dynamic properties of LoRAs, we must take necessary steps to ensure the optimizations we apply are robust.

For example, we can apply torch.compile on a model loaded with a particular LoRA to obtain speedups on inference latency. However, the moment we swap out the LoRA with a different one (with a potentially different configuration), we will run into recompilation complications, causing slowdowns in inference.

Industry observers note that one can also fuse the LoRA parameters into the base model parameters, run compilation, and unfuse the LoRA parameters when loading new ones. However, this approach will again encounter the problem of recompilation whenever inference is run, due to potential architecture-level changes.

Our optimization recipe takes into account the above-mentioned situations to be as realistic as possible. Below are the key components of our optimization recipe:.

Sources indicate that note that amongst the above-mentioned, FP8 quantization is lossy but often provides the most formidable speed-memory trade-off. Even though we tested the recipe primarily using NVIDIA GPUs, it should work on AMD GPUs, too.

Industry observers note that in our previous blog posts (post 1 and post 2), we have already discussed the benefits of using the first three components of our optimization recipe. Applying them one by one is just a few lines of code:.

The FA3 processor comes from here.

The problems start surfacing when we try to swap in and swap out LoRAs into a compiled diffusion transformer (pipe.transformer) without triggering recompilation.

Normally, loading and unloading LoRAs will require recompilation, which defeats any speed advantage gained from compilation. Thankfully, there is a way to avoid the need for recompilation. By passing hotswap=True, diffusers will leave the model architecture unchanged and only exchange the weights of the LoRA adapter itself, which does not necessitate recompilation.

(As a reminder, the first call to pipe will be slow as torch.compile is a just-in-time compiler. However, the subsequent calls should be significantly faster.).

This generally allows for swapping LoRAs without recompilation, but there are limitations:.

For more information on hotswapping in Diffusers and its limitations, visit the hotswapping section of the documentation.

The benefits of this workflow become evident when we look at the inference latency without using compilation with hotswapping.

The optimization recipe we have discussed so far assumes access to a powerful GPU like H100. However, what can we do when we’re limited to using consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090? Let’s find out.

Sources indicate that flux.1-Dev (without any LoRA), using the Bfloat16 data-type, takes ~33GB of memory to run. Depending on the size of the LoRA module, and without using any optimization, this memory footprint can increase even further. Many consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 only have 24GB. Throughout the rest of this section, we will consider an RTX 4090 machine as our testbed.

According to recent reports, first, to enable end-to-end execution of Flux.1-Dev, we can apply CPU offloading wherein components that are not needed to execute the current computation are offloaded to the CPU to free more accelerator memory. Doing so allows us to run the entire pipeline in ~22GB in 35.403 seconds on an RTX 4090. Enabling compilation can reduce the latency down to 31.205 seconds (1.12x speedup). In terms of code, it’s just a few lines:.

It has been revealed that notice that we didn’t apply the FP8 quantization here because it’s not supported with CPU offloading and compilation (supporting glitch thread). Therefore, just applying FP8 quantization to the Flux Transformer isn’t enough to mitigate the memory exhaustion problem, either. In this instance, we decided to remove it.

Recent findings suggest that therefore, to take advantage of the FP8 quantization scheme, we need to find a way to do it without CPU offloading. For Flux.1-Dev, if we additionally apply quantization to the T5 text encoder, we should be able to load and run the complete pipeline in 24GB. Below is a comparison of the results with and without the T5 text encoder being quantized (NF4 quantization from bitsandbytes).

Sources indicate that as we can notice in the figure above, quantizing the T5 text encoder doesn’t incur too much of a quality loss. Combining the quantized T5 text encoder and FP8-quantized Flux Transformer with torch.compile gives us somewhat reasonable results – 9.668 seconds from 32.27 seconds (a massive ~3.3x speedup) without a noticeable quality drop.

It is possible to generate images with 24 GB of VRAM even without quantizing the T5 text encoder, but that would have made our generation pipeline slightly more complicated.

We now have a way to run the entire Flux.1-Dev pipeline with FP8 quantization on an RTX 4090. We can apply the previously established optimization recipe for optimizing LoRA inference on the same hardware. Since FA3 isn’t supported on RTX 4090, we will stick to the following optimization recipe with T5 quantization newly added to the mix:.

In the table below, we show the inference latency numbers with different combinations of the above components applied.

To enable hotswapping without triggering recompilation, two hurdles have to be overcome. First, the LoRA scaling factor has to be converted into torch tensors from floats, which is achieved fairly easily. Second, the shape of the LoRA weights needs to padded to the largest required shape. That way, the data in the weights can be replaced without the need to reassign the whole attribute. This is why the max_rank argument discussed above is crucial. As we pad the values with zeros, the results remain unchanged, although the computation is slowed down a bit depending on how large the padding is.

It has been revealed that since no upcoming LoRA attributes are added, this also requires that each LoRA after the first one can only target the same layers, or a subset of layers, that the first one targets. Thus, choose the order of loading wisely. If LoRAs target disjoint layers, there is the possibility to create a dummy LoRA that targets the union of all target layers.

To see the nitty-gritty of this implementation, visit the hotswap.py file in PEFT.

This post outlined an optimization recipe for fast LoRA inference with Flux, demonstrating significant speedups. Our approach combines Flash Attention 3, torch.compile, and FP8 quantization while ensuring hotswapping capabilities without recompilation challenges. On high-end GPUs like the H100, this optimized setup provides a 2.23x speedup over the baseline.

For consumer GPUs, specifically the RTX 4090, we tackled memory limitations by introducing T5 text encoder quantization (NF4) and leveraging regional compilation. This comprehensive recipe achieved a substantial 2.04x speedup, making LoRA inference on Flux viable and performant even with limited VRAM. The key insight is that by carefully managing compilation and quantization, the benefits of LoRA can be fully realized across different hardware configurations.

Hopefully, the recipes from this post will inspire you to optimize your LoRA-based use cases, benefitting from speedy inference.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (400 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight.
  • They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules.
  • Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

According to recent reports, today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

Recent findings suggest that if the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a blueprint, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

Industry observers note that compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same company that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera.

Industry observers note that slideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only highlights up in one out of every 64 boxes.

It has been revealed that the E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS.

Connect instantly via Bluetooth to the KODAK Memory Link App. From live slideshows and custom QR codes to countdowns and dual-network tracking with Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub, the KODAK SlideTag seamlessly integrates retro aesthetics into your everyday carry.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and indicates which setting to change for your app.

Industry observers note that I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Every server got the same requests:.

Sources indicate that ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

Sources indicate that the tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Sources indicate that ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code says so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

It has been revealed that A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next highlights.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

According to recent reports, the obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

In a recent development, the cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ says the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

That context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps revealed 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:.

Sources indicate that the price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

In a recent development, in Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

The last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many users, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

All figures are total tokens per second.

With its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds fresh requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Recent findings suggest that total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:.

Sources indicate that for a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:.

If you run an older llama.cpp, upgrade first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a new CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

It reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:.

Setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

In a recent development, it starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

It also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

All four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:.

In Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:.

Qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, none of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

Sources indicate that before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your consumers' wait more than the choice of engine.

Sources indicate that not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Recent findings suggest that ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

In a recent development, when many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

Recent findings suggest that usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

#172207. TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • Recent findings suggest that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

Recent findings suggest that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

This measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

The promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

In a recent development, in practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

TimeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

According to recent reports, figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

This tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

It has been revealed that here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

Industry observers note that for questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

Example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and reveals that performance drops as the video gets longer.

To kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Sources indicate that model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

In a recent development, gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

According to recent reports, trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

TimeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.

Home Office needs more time with the PNC, which began life more than 50 years ago.

Industry observers note that * Updated to add: A source close to the matter told The Register there is an agreement in place for support of the database software, however the Home Office would not comment. We first asked about the support contract several days prior to the publication of this article. The Register has filed a Freedom of Information request to compel the government to clarify the matter.*The UK’s Home Office has been unable to provide evidence to show how the Police National Computer (PNC) is getting vendor support for three years or more after it missed another deadline to decommission the aging crime-fighting system first introduced in 1974.

The PNC was first released in 1974, when Tom Baker began his iconic role playing Doctor Who, and has seen the tenure of 26 UK Home Secretaries, surviving multiple efforts to replace it.

It has been revealed that A notice in December 2024 stated that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." We understand that PNC support refers to the Fujitsu support contract for the mainframe, which is housed in north London. Support for the Software AG database on the mainframe OS (BS2000) ran out at the end of 2024. So the database holding the crucial police data remains out of standard support and potentially will stay that way until 2027.The decommissioning date for the PNC had already been pushed back by the need to delay and "reset" the LEDS in 2020. The Home Office launched its successor, National Law Enforcement Data Service, in 2016, and planned to finish the new system by 2020 at a cost of £671 million.

The Home Office told The Register this week that it needed more time, and it aimed to begin decommissioning the system from March 2027, raising questions over how it would be supported.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We are modernizing policing systems to adapt to evolving challenges, including rolling out the LEDS to replace the Police National Computer.

"While LEDS is already operational, we are continuing to run the legacy Police National Computer system to support the operational needs of all UK police," they said.

Officials said the PNC would remain available throughout the transition and would only be disconnected when police forces have confirmed that they no longer need it.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, in a written response in the House of Lords, Lord Hanson of Flint, a junior minister, said the PNC might be required until early 2028. Some LEDS services were already live and the program was "targeting completion of the remaining development, adoption and readiness activity in early 2027 as we prepare for our final stages for LEDS deployment before retiring the PNC," he said.

Industry observers note that "Once the transition of all police people to the LEDS has been completed and policing has confirmed that the PNC is no longer required, the system will be disconnected and decommissioned. The decommissioning process is expected to take place between late 2027 and early 2028," he noted.

It has been revealed that according to the National Audit Office (NAO), the PNC is the most important national policing information system in the UK. It serves front-line officers from all 45 local police forces, as well as by 127 other organisations that need to access its data. In 2019-20, the police searched or updated the PNC 133 million times.

The ongoing delay to the decommissioning of the PNC raises questions about how — and whether — it is being adequately supported.

The PNC is sited at a datacenter in Hendon, North London, and is based on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe, but this is technology originally developed by German engineering outfit Siemens inherited by Fujitsu when it acquired the data processing division of that company.

It was the subject of controversy in 2021 when an error led to the accidental loss of 413,000 records of police evidence from the system, the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records targeted for deletion, although the lost data was eventually recovered.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Fujitsu — the Japanese tech giant at the center of the Post Office Horizon scandal — was awarded a £48 million ($56.6 million) renewed contract for support and maintenance of the PNC after no other companies tendered for the work. The contract was set to expire in March 2026.

In its 2021 report, NAO mentioned the Fujitsu mainframe computer used by the PNC would reach the end of its supported life by 31 December 2021.

"The Software AG database used by the PNC is only supported on the Fujitsu mainframe until 31 December 2023. The Department has an option to extend the contract for this support for a further 12 months but it has not yet agreed this with the supplier. If [the replacement system] is not ready, the PNC will need to be moved off the mainframe onto a supported operating system from 2025 or run unsupported," the report mentioned.

However, at the time, the Home Office told the NAO it had decided to accept the risk of running the PNC without support for the database for 12 months after December 2024. "This would leave the PNC at higher risk of disruption for at least a year, although the Department's view is that the actual risk profile is low because of the mitigation actions put in place," the report stated [PDF].

It added that moving the PNC to a latest operating system could take three years and Home Office estimated that it will cost at least £30 million, including the cost of rewriting code for the new OS.

A report from the Public Accounts Committee later in November 2021 mentioned: "The team that maintains the PNC is under-resourced and several staff are nearing retirement… The Department currently intends to run this piece of critical national infrastructure without full manufacturer support for the database after 2024, meaning it will not have that support for at least a year, though the Department plans to provide in-house support instead.".

According to recent reports, unless the Home Office has come up with another plan in the meantime, it is set to extend that out-of-support period to around three years. It has been offered the opportunity to provide additional comment. ®.
