Kit piggybacks off TV and mobile signals and can be neatly stuffed into an SUV.

BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position.

The defense biz states its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal.

Sources indicate that conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies.

Passive radar is not fresh, but BAE indicates its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV.

Industry observers note that BAE states it can track targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft and provides a clear 3D air picture with data such as target speed, heading, range and altitude. This could make it suitable for law enforcement agencies and for guarding critical national infrastructure, as well as military consumers.

BAE pitches the system for sites such as airports, where avoiding interference with existing equipment matters. Because it doesn't transmit its own radar signal, passive radar avoids adding another broadcast to the mix.

"While people are sat at home watching TV, our new radar technology can use transmissions from those TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," claims BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd.

The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says.

Industry observers note that elsewhere at BAE Systems, the news is less rosy: The Financial Times reports that it intends to shed more than 1,000 jobs at its head office and air division in the UK. The tech giant states the cuts will help it become more agile and meet government demands for "greater speed and efficiency" in delivering critical defense products. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters.
  • These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.
  • We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters. In TRL, we already demonstrated how to post-train VLMs with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This time, we’re going further.

tl;dr Here’s what’s fresh in TRL:.

These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.

This enables more efficient and scalable multimodal alignment.

In a recent development, traditionally, you would take a base model, apply SFT to follow instructions, and then apply DPO to align it to preferential data. Previously, we adapted this approach to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and validated it on IDEFICS2, showing improvement in model responses.

DPO works by optimizing preferences between pairs of model responses using a contrastive loss: you have a chosen and a rejected answer and you optimize your preferences based on what you want and don’t want.

Recent findings suggest that but in the last year, fresh multimodal alignment methods have gained popularity, GRPO and MPO, that can push VLM performance even further. At the end of the blog post you can find a table that showcases the differences between model responses.

Recent findings suggest that aligning multimodal models with SFT to do reasoning tasks falls short due to distribution shift. Meanwhile, models aligned with DPO fail to generate coherent rationales and might generate repetitive responses. To address this, there’s a newly introduced technique called Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) specifically made for multimodal models. This method is essentially an extension of DPO with multiple losses: preference loss from DPO (sigmoid), quality loss from Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), and generation loss from SFT. According to the paper, simply switching to this combined loss results in 6.2 pts improvement in MathVista!

Since this is only modifying the loss, we added combined loss support to TRL's DPOTrainer class. To use it, you can initialize the DPOConfig as follows:.

Then initialize the DPOTrainer:.

And that’s it! If you want to explore further, you can find a complete notebook example here.

Recent findings suggest that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a cutting-edge alignment method initially introduced in DeepSeek Math paper and later integrated to DeepSeek R1, the groundbreaking LLM. It’s an addition to PPO where the policy updates are done over groups (batches of trajectories that represent how a dialogue rolls out). This feature makes it more robust to reward noise, as the noise averages out within groups. Since the model learns broader sense of a good response rather than singular high reward samples, this method also makes the model highly performant.

In TRL, we now introduce GRPO support for vision language models. We will not provide a full training script example, as you can find it in the notebook. Instead, we'll focus on highlighting the key component and concepts.

To make the training script work effectively, we need to validate that the format of the answer is correct and that the solution itself is close to the completed parts, so we write two reward functions. In order to really see improvements in the latter reward, you would need a rather maximalist setup, where you have relatively larger models, a lot of generations, and a high-quality, diverse dataset.

Then, you can initialize GRPOConfig and GRPOTrainer, pass in the reward functions we defined above and call train() to start training.

Explore the full notebook example here.

Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) is a RL alignment algorithm recently released by Qwen that overcomes some limitations of GRPO. It achieves a more stable training computing importance sampling weights at the sequence level instead of per-token. Its benefits are more relevant in MoE style models.

Latest TRL also introduces support for GSPO and since it’s a variant of GRPO's loss, it comes with multimodal support. To create the trainer, the process is the same as with GRPO, but adding the following extra params (values are extracted from the paper).

In addition to MPO, GRPO, and GSPO, TRL now supports Reinforce Leave One Out (RLOO) and Online Direct Preference Optimization (Online DPO) for Vision Language Models (VLMs), enabling alignment on multimodal datasets.

With the standardization of the transformers API, we have shipped a full support for vision language models. You can simply initialize SFTTrainer with a VLM.

It has been revealed that to train a VLM, you need to provide a dataset with an additional images column containing the images to be processed. You can take a look at Dataset Formats — Vision Datasets for more information on how it should look like. A good example is LLaVA Instruct Mix.

As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.
  • The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.
  • An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.

The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.

An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop, is available online.

To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job.

If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more.

PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It states the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012.

In a recent development, even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion.

A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships.

According to recent reports, the advocacy group wants to see legislators take this issue in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools.

Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the problem is.

DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools.

“We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” notes Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report.

Sources indicate that “We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for manuals, diagnostic tools, secure access and more. Not only are all these tolls expensive, they also create traffic jams, slowing down the whole process, which adds to the costs for consumers.”  ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MGM Resorts and BetMGM have canceled their memberships in the National Council on Problem Gambling because the group accepted Kalshi.
  • The companies’ letter to the council is dated Nov.
  • The companies wrote that they no longer hold the principles the group once stood for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MGM Resorts and BetMGM have canceled their memberships in the National Council on Problem Gambling because the group accepted Kalshi. Their exit brings licensed operators into a split over prediction markets that had so far involved regulators and state problem-gambling councils.

The companies’ letter to the council is dated Nov. 18. Stephen Martino, MGM Resorts’ senior vice president and chief compliance officer, signed it alongside Rhea Loney, BetMGM’s chief compliance officer. It went to interim executive director Charles Jeffers and board president Derek Longmeier.

The companies wrote that they no longer hold the principles the group once stood for. They argued that promoting gambling as a way out of financial trouble runs against responsible gaming principles. The letter also charged that Kalshi disregards state gambling laws when it sells sports event contracts in states whose regulators consider them unlicensed gambling.

According to recent reports, MGM and BetMGM are the first gambling operators to confirm they left specifically over the council’s work with Kalshi, SBC Americas reported. The Ohio Casino Control Commission had already ended its membership. Michigan had won a temporary restraining order against Kalshi on June 29, 2026. The Nevada Council on Problem Gambling and Washington’s Evergreen Council on Problem Gambling also left.

The council announced the deal at the center of the dispute on May 18, 2026. Besides its funding commitment, Kalshi received a seat in the NCPG’s Leadership Circle. That group is made up of top partners that help fund the organization.

Recent findings suggest that the Nov. 18 letter sets out the main grievances licensed operators hold against prediction markets. Kalshi lets 18-year-olds trade. Most licensed sportsbooks require bettors to be 21. Prediction markets pay little in state taxes, which leaves less money for problem-gambling programs. They also sit outside state self-exclusion programs.

Each of those points touches the core work of a harm-reduction body. The fight over whether prediction markets count as gambling has now reached the main US problem-gambling group.

“No organization should understand the risks Kalshi and other prediction markets pose to responsible gaming more clearly and urgently than NCPG,”– MGM/BetMGM while ending membership in the National Council on Problem Gambling.https://t.co/7A0Wi2AIFo via @reviewjournal.

— David Danzis (@AC2Vegas_Danzis) November 22, 2026.

The NCPG has not backed down. The group describes its prediction-market work as a way to tackle new sources of gambling harm. It says that work does not endorse particular companies or how they do business. In a Friday statement, the NCPG remarked the risks of prediction markets will not go away when organizations refuse to engage. It added that leaving over this work may send a political message but does nothing to prevent gambling-related harm.

Accelerate ND-Parallel: A guide to Efficient Multi-GPU Training

📅 08 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies.
  • We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.
  • According to recent reports, to further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies. In Accelerate, together with Axolotl, we have integrated a quick and easy way to use any combination of parallelism strategies in your training script!

Here is how to add it to your training script:.

We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.

According to recent reports, to further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl. To help you get started right away we've tested some example configs which you can modify to suit your needs - try one out with:.

You can also check out the Axolotl ND-Parallelism docs for more details - adding ND parallel techniques to your existing configs is as simple as adding one or more of the following fields to your Axolotl config file:.

We've made it easy to configure the degrees of different parallelism strategies and how they are combined through the ParallelismConfig class in Accelerate, or through config fields in Axolotl, but how do we know which configuration will work best for our use case? As we scale to training models with tens or even hundreds of billions of parameters, the primary challenge comes from understanding the different parallelism strategies and how they interact to minimise communication overhead across devices. In this post, we'll walk through how the different parallelism strategies work, and when and how you might want to compose them.

According to recent reports, data parallelism (DP) is the most common technique for training models across multiple GPUs, and involves replicating the model, gradients and optimizer states across each device, whilst evenly distributing data batches between GPUs, and synchronising gradients across devices before updating parameters. This can significantly increase throughput compared to single-device training, but requires that your model is able to fit on a single device.

According to recent reports, we can control the number of replicas of the model with the dp_replicate_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or config field in Axolotl. It's worth noting that DP is a top-most-level parallelism strategy, meaning that if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and we compose it with other parallelism strategies, there would be 2 replicas of the model, each also influenced by the other parallelism strategies. For example, if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and tp_size=2, we would have 2 replicas of the model, each with 2 tensor parallel shards.

We use the term shard to describe data on a single device which is a partition of a larger piece of data.

Sources indicate that what if our model is too large to fit on a single device? Fully sharded data parallel (FSDP) addresses this issue by sharding (distributing evenly) the model’s weights, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs (this is inspired by DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-3), whilst each device still receives its portion of the full batch of data. As you may notice from the diagram above, rather than requiring a full copy of the entire model on each device, we only gather the weights for a single layer at a time before the forward pass, after which the weights may be sharded again.

Sources indicate that in this way, we trade memory usage for the communication overhead of gathering sharded parameters before each forward and backward pass, and reduce-scatter-ing local gradients. We can control this trade-off in FSDP by tuning the granularity at which parameters are gathered. On one extreme, we can gather and re-shard every layer of our model, which would result in the lowest peak memory usage, but incur the highest communication costs. In practice, a common approach is to gather the weights for an entire transformer decoder block at a time.

Industry observers note that whilst we can make further memory-compute trade-offs and offload model parameters and gradients to the CPU to train larger models, this can be prohibitively slow. Instead, let’s consider how we can effectively utilise even more devices to train larger models whilst maintaining high data throughput.

In a recent development, we use the term node to refer to a single machine which hosts multiple GPUs (up to a maximum of 8), with fast intra-node communication channels using e.g. NVLink between GPUs. When using multiple nodes for training, we rely on relatively slower inter-node communication channels between machines using e.g. Infiniband. We also refer to the total number of devices in the process pool as the world size - e.g. a single node with 8 GPUs represents a world size of 8, and 4 nodes would represent a world size of 32.

In a recent development, when using FSDP across multiple nodes, we treat the entire set of devices across nodes as if we were training on a single node. For example, with 4 nodes containing 8 GPUs each, we perform our sharding across 32 devices, and perform our collective all-reduce and reduce-scatter operations using both inter-and-intra-node communication backends. In this manner, FSDP alone can scale to a substantial number of GPUs with a large global batch size to increase data throughput. However, there comes a point where several challenges arise that may require composing FSDP with other parallelism techniques. We usually try to avoid doing FSDP across more than a full node, as the communication overhead can become too high, we'll talk about how to address this in the section on Hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism.

You can use the dp_shard_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig together with a prepared FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin, or set the dp_shard_size config field in Axolotl to set the degree of FSDP applied to your model.

According to recent reports, tensor Parallel (TP) is a kind of model parallelism technique, where shards of the model permanently live on separate devices, and in contrast to data parallel techniques, each device receives an identical batch of data. TP works by distributing the computation of linear layers across devices, so each device only computes a portion of the matrix multiplication. This technique works best when there are large linear layers, such as the feed-forward layers in transformer models, which can be split across devices. We can also use TP on each of the query, key, value, and output projections in the attention layers with almost no extra communication cost.

To achieve the best performance, parameters of consecutive layers can be distributed in a specific fashion, minimizing the required communication. When working with pairs of linear layers, we can split the first layer column-wise, and the subsequent layer row-wise, allowing us to compute the output with only a single all-reduce operation to combine the sharded outputs.

Unlike the dynamic sharding behaviour of FSDP, TP creates static memory partitions which result in a constant memory usage reduction scaling with the TP group size. This becomes crucial for massive models where even a single decoder layer is too large to fit into memory during the FSDP all-gather (recall that common practice in FSDP is to gather the weights of an entire decoder layer at a time). However, unlike FSDP which scales relatively linearly across nodes (up to a point - ~512 GPUs on a homogenous cluster, significantly less across lower-bandwidth connections), TP is only effective within the boundaries of a single node. TP requires frequent activation synchronization between devices during computation, as each device computes only a portion of the output, requiring the outputs from other devices to be communicated before continuing the forward pass. Thus, if we wish to utilise TP in a multi-node setup, we must consider composing TP with other parallelism techniques, while keeping TP only within a single node. Due to its large communications overhead, TP is not recommended for PCIe linked GPUs.

In Accelerate, the TP size is configured through tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the tensor_parallel_size config field.

Industry observers note that recently, reasoning capabilities in LLMs resulted in sequence lengths skyrocketing as models use more and more tokens to solve complex tasks. To achieve this behaviour through fine-tuning, we need a way to train models on very large sequence lengths - which can sometimes reach up to a million tokens!

It has been revealed that since the attention operation in transformers scales quadratically with context length, this becomes impossible on a single GPU. For example, when fine-tuning a relatively small model such as Mistral-7B (which uses 32 attention heads), if we use a sequence length of 128k a single attention matrix will utilise 128k * 128k * 2 bytes * num_heads=32 = ~32GB * 32 = ~1TB of activations memory! Whilst this example is not realistic when using optimised attention implementations such as FlashAttention, it helps illustrate the growth in memory requirements from increasing the context length.

With context parallelism (CP), we can shard the inputs across the sequence dimension, resulting in each device only processing a chunk of the full context and computing a smaller portion of the full, prohibitively large, attention matrix. To see how this works, recall that the attention computation is described by the equation: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}(QK^T)V Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V.

In a recent development, where Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V are the query, key, and value matrices respectively. Each query vector (row, or input embedding) of Q Q Q must compute the attention scores against every key vector of K K K in the entire sequence to correctly apply the softmax normalisation. These attention scores are then weighted with all value vectors in V V V.

According to recent reports, the crucial detail here lies in the fact that each row in Q Q Q can compute its attention score independently of one another, but each query vector still requires the full K K K and V V V matrices. In other words, given an input with sequence length $n$, we can expand our above attention equation as:.

Attention(Q,K,V)1=softmax(Q1KT)VAttention(Q,K,V)2=softmax(Q2KT)V⋮Attention(Q,K,V)n=softmax(QnKT)V \begin{align} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_1 &= \text{softmax}(Q_1 K^T) V \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_2 &= \text{softmax}(Q_2 K^T) V \\ &\vdots \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_n &= \text{softmax}(Q_n K^T) V \end{align} Attention(Q,K,V)1​Attention(Q,K,V)2​Attention(Q,K,V)n​​=softmax(Q1​KT)V=softmax(Q2​KT)V⋮=softmax(Qn​KT)V​​.

where we denote each row of the query matrix as Q1,Q2,...,Qn Q_1, Q_2, ..., Q_n Q1​,Q2​,...,Qn​. This can be generalized as: Attention(Q,K,V)i=softmax(QiKT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_i = \text{softmax}(Q_i K^T) V \quad \forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., n\} Attention(Q,K,V)i​=softmax(Qi​KT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n}.

Industry observers note that when we shard the inputs across devices, the resulting Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V matrices (computed from these input shards) are also automatically sharded along the sequence dimension - each GPU computes queries, keys, and values only for its portion of the sequence. For example, with a world size of W W W GPUs and sequence length n n n:.

Recent findings suggest that how do we ensure the attention is computed correctly? As established above, each device only needs its own shard of Q Q Q, but requires the full K K K and V V V matrices to compute the attention correctly. We can achieve this by using a technique called RingAttention, which works as follows:.

Accelerate enables this with the accelerator.maybe_context_parallel decorator, which is also showcased in the Accelerate example script. You can also learn more about how it works and its limitations in our CP concept guide.

Similar to TP, in Accelerate the CP size is configured through cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the context_parallel_size config field.

Sources indicate that in the multi-node setting, data parallel techniques such as FSDP treat the entire network topology as if it existed along a single dimension. You may find this approach limiting for a variety of reasons:.

It has been revealed that to try and address some of these problems, we can think of multi-node clusters as having a two-dimensional topology: fast intra-node communication between devices along one axis, and relatively slower inter-node communication along another axis. Let’s consider how we can compose the parallelism techniques we’ve introduced so far to take advantage of this.

Sources indicate that hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism (HSDP) is a kind of 2D parallelism which performs FSDP within a node, and DP across nodes - that is to say the model is replicated across each node, and sharded using FSDP within each node. This allows the greater communication overhead of FSDP to utilize the faster intra-node links, whilst DP minimises the slower inter-node communication overhead to a single gradient synchronisation step. You might consider this approach if you were facing problem 1 and wished to speed up training at the cost of increased memory usage.

It’s crucial to note that we can freely configure the shape of our 2D network topology, as we aren’t constrained to the dimensions being aligned with physical node boundaries - you might apply FSDP across 2 nodes whilst replicating across groups of 2 nodes, which would result in lower memory usage but slower throughput, but still reduce the intra-node FSDP communication overhead by a factor of two. This is a knob we encourage you to tune to your specific hardware setup and fine-tuning needs.

You can enable HSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and dp_replicate_size in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or through Axolotl's config fields.

It has been revealed that as we mentioned earlier, TP should be applied within a node to utilize the high-bandwidth intra-node communications, thus, combining TP and FSDP involves sharding the model across nodes using FSDP, and within a node using TP. To a certain degree, this potentially offers a neat solution to all three of the issues above: the latency costs from FSDP could be reduced by a factor of 8, layers that are too large to fit on a single device are now evenly distributed across devices, and since each TP group receives an identical batch of data, we can also reduce our global batch size by a factor of 8. However, if this remains insufficient, we are unable to increase the TP size across nodes and must consider an alternative approach.

In Accelerate you can combine TP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

In a recent development, this is a 2D parallelism strategy that combines FSDP and CP, and while this is not very commonly used as CP already combines with FSDP (more on why in the accelerate concept guide), it can be useful in some cases i.e. when requiring a large sequence length, consequently requiring a large cp_size. If this still doesn't fit into your memory budget, you can apply FSDP on top of this, further reducing the memory usage.

In Accelerate you can combine CP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and context_parallel_size config fields.

With a sufficiently large world size (note: while the minimum world size for 3D parallelism is 8, it is most effective at much larger scales), we can consider combining HSDP with TP which creates a hierarchy where DP first replicates the model across groups of nodes, FSDP then shards the model within each group, and TP splits individual layers within each node. You might consider this approach when facing all of the scaling constraints we mentioned above, as it provides the most flexibility to adapt to your specific training setup by making trade-offs between memory usage and throughput.

According to recent reports, in Accelerate you can combine HSDP and TP by defining all of dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tp_size in ParallelismConfig. Similarly in Axolotl you can add all of the dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

There are additional ways to combine multiple parallelisms which we haven't covered, such as 4D parallel using HSDP + TP + CP, but they operate very similarly to the techniques we've already covered. Most of all, we encourage you to play with different techniques and configurations - this is the best way to gain an intuition for the different ways in which you can make memory/throughput trade-offs.

Below are some additional tips you may find useful when working in distributed settings:.

Industry observers note that when using FSDP and working with models that are too large to fit in a single device, enabling both CPU RAM efficient loading and sharded state dict checkpointing technique is crucial. You can enable this through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type parameters in Accelerate's FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin,.

or through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type config fields inside the fsdp_config in Axolotl:.

The total batch size used during training plays an important factor in training stability, memory usage, and data throughput. When using DP and/or FSDP the effective batch size is calculated as:.

effective_batch_size = micro_batch_size * gradient_accumulation_steps * dp_world_size.

where dp_world_size = (dp_shard_size * dp_replicate_size) / tp_size. You can increase your batch size by increasing your total micro batch size or gradient accumulation steps in your training loop, or setting the micro_batch_size and gradient_accumulation_steps config fields in Axolotl, or increasing the total dp_world_size by adding more GPUs. As we mentioned above, this imposes a minimum total batch size of dp_world_size - when using pure DP/FSDP, this will be your total world size, and if this is too high the only way to decrease the total batch size is by introducing tensor parallelism. Finally, with a fixed number of GPUs and in memory-constrained scenarios, we recommend increasing gradient_accumulation_steps instead of micro_batch_size to achieve larger effective batch sizes, and vice-versa.

Recent findings suggest that correspondingly, when your effective batch size increases due to introducing data parallelism, you should scale your learning rate to maintain training stability. Common approaches include linear scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * (effective_batch_size / base_batch_size) or square root scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * sqrt(effective_batch_size / base_batch_size).

When memory constraints persist even with parallelism strategies, gradient checkpointing can provide additional memory savings by trading compute for memory. During the forward pass, only a subset of activations are kept in memory (typically at transformer block boundaries), and intermediate activations are recomputed during the backward pass. This technique works seamlessly with all parallelism strategies covered above. In Accelerate, you can enable it by setting activation_checkpointing=true in FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin:.

Note that gradient checkpointing typically increases training time by ~20-30% due to activation recomputation, but can reduce activation memory by 60-80%, making it particularly valuable when training very large models or using long sequence lengths.

Hi, presently it's only available if you use fsdp2 too, as the composability without fsdp2 is limited (will change in next release). You can use accelerate config in the command line to specify it.

Google claims last week’s critical VMware bug was under attack in September

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China-linked ARMORY CASTLE knew about it weeks before it unleashed five custom malware tools targeting vCenter.
  • Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.
  • According to recent reports, VMware revealed several flaws on November 19.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China-linked ARMORY CASTLE knew about it weeks before it unleashed five custom malware tools targeting vCenter.

Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.

According to recent reports, VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The major nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs.

According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust.

Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks.

Recent findings suggest that if the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.”.

Sources indicate that the gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.”.

Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter.

It has been revealed that and BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its strategy to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE.

“The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also demonstrates the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.”.

Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on.

Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW.

The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890.

A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.”.

VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite.

In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases.

“Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report.

One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription.

VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.”.

In a recent development, readers have pointed out that information about the upcoming cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies.

A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post.

Industry observers note that “Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®.

It has been revealed that hugging Face AI Sheets is a upcoming, open-source tool for building, enriching, and transforming datasets using AI models with no code. The tool can be deployed locally or on the Hub. It lets you use thousands of open models from the Hugging Face Hub via Inference Providers or local models, including gpt-oss from OpenAI!

Try the tool for free (no installation required): https://huggingface.co/spaces/aisheets/sheetsInstall and run locally: https://github.com/huggingface/sheets.

According to recent reports, AI Sheets is a no-code tool for building, transforming, and enriching datasets using (open) AI models. It’s tightly integrated with the Hub and the open-source AI ecosystem.

AI Sheets uses an easy-to-learn user interface, similar to a spreadsheet. The tool is built around quick experimentation, starting with small datasets before running long/costly data generation pipelines.

Sources indicate that in AI Sheets, newly introduced columns are created by writing prompts, and you can iterate as many times as you need and edit the cells/validate cells to teach the model what you want. But more on this later!

Recent findings suggest that compare and vibe test models. Imagine you want to test the latest models on your data. You can import a dataset with prompts/questions, and create several columns (one per model) with a prompt like this: Answer the following: {{prompt}}, where prompt is a column in your dataset. You can validate the results manually or create a new column with an LLM as a judge prompt like this: Evaluate the responses to the following question: {{prompt}}. Response 1: {{model1}}. Response 2: {{model2}}, where model1 and model2 are columns in your dataset with different model responses.

Recent findings suggest that improve prompts for your data and specific models. Imagine you want to build an application to process customer requests and give automatic answers. You can load a sample dataset with customer requests and start playing and iterating with different prompts and models to generate responses. One cool feature of AI Sheets is that you can provide feedback by editing or validating cells. These example cells will be added to your prompts automatically. You can think of it as a tool to fine-tune prompts and add a few-shot examples to your prompts very efficiently, by looking at your data in real-time!

Recent findings suggest that transform a dataset. Imagine you want to clean up a column of your dataset. You can add a upcoming column with a prompt like Remove extra punctuation marks from the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to clean up.

Recent findings suggest that classify a dataset. Imagine you want to classify some content in your dataset. You can add a newly introduced column with a prompt like Categorize the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to categorize.

It has been revealed that analyze a dataset. Imagine you want to extract the main ideas in your dataset. You can add a new column with a prompt like this: Extract the most notable ideas from the following: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to analyze.

Enrich a dataset. Imagine you have a dataset with addresses that are missing zip codes. You can add a latest column with a prompt like this: Find the zip code of the following address: {{address}} (in this case, you must enable the "Search the web" option to ensure accurate results).

In a recent development, generate a synthetic dataset. Imagine you need a dataset with realistic emails, but the data is not available for data privacy reasons. Then you can create another column with a prompt like this Write a realistic professional email as it was written by the following person: {{person_bio}}.

Best for: Familiarizing with AI Sheets, brainstorming, rapid experiments, and creating test datasets.

Recent findings suggest that conference talks fail on slides more often than on content. The speaker knows the material and has something worth saying, but the deck is a wall of bullets, or a template everyone in the room has seen before, or forty slides for a twenty-minute slot. AI presentation makers can now produce a complete deck from an outline in minutes, which solves the time problem and creates a new one: the output tends toward exactly the uniform, stock-image, bullet-heavy style that audiences have learned to tune out.

This article explains how conference slides differ from other decks, why AI-generated decks look generic and what specifically causes it, a workflow that uses an AI presentation maker for speed while keeping the talk distinctive, how to handle the slide types that matter most in a talk (the opening, the demonstration, the data, the close), and a checklist to run before the talk.

In a recent development, A conference talk is spoken, timed and performed to a room. That changes the rules compared with a reading deck or a business presentation.

The causes are specific and therefore fixable.

Template uniformity. Every slide uses the same layout family, so the deck has no visual rhythm. Audiences read the sameness as mass-produced.

Industry observers note that bullet default. Given a paragraph, the tool produces three to five bullets. Given twenty paragraphs, twenty bullet slides.

Stock imagery. Icons and photos chosen by keyword match the topic superficially and add no meaning. A talk about database indexing gets a picture of a filing cabinet.

Label titles. “Introduction”, “Background”, “Key Challenges”, “Conclusion”. Titles that name the category rather than make the point.

Sources indicate that flattened emphasis. The tool does not know which of your ideas is the one the audience should leave with, so every slide gets equal weight.

Recent findings suggest that no pacing. Every slide carries the same amount of content, so there is no build, no pause, no payoff.

Each of these is a default that can be overridden, either in how the input is prepared or in a short editing pass afterwards.

Step 1: Write the talk before the slides. Not a script necessarily, but the argument: what the audience knows at the start, what they know at the end, and the four to six moves that get them there. Write the one sentence you want them to repeat to a colleague afterwards. If this is not clear, no deck will fix it.

Step 2: Write the slide titles as the things you will say. Each title is a sentence, in your voice, that states the point of that moment in the talk. “Indexes make reads fast by making writes slower” is a title. “Index trade-offs” is not. Read the titles in order; they should be the talk in miniature.

Recent findings suggest that step 3: Mark the pacing. Next to each title, note whether the slide is a hold (a key point, stays up while you talk for a minute or more), a beat (a quick slide in a sequence), or a reveal (something shown, a demo, a result). This tells you where to put effort.

Step 4: Generate. Paste the titles with one or two sentences of content under each into an ai presentation maker. Ask for a slide count close to your title count. Pick the plainest theme available; distinctiveness will come from your content, not the template.

Step 5: Strip the bullets. On every hold slide, delete the bullets and leave the title, or the title plus one image or one number. On beat slides, keep at most one short line. The content that was in the bullets goes into speaker notes, which is where it belonged.

It has been revealed that step 6: Replace every stock image. Delete icons. Replace keyword-matched photos with your own material: a screenshot, a diagram you drew, a chart from your data, a photograph you took, a single large word. If a slide has no genuine visual, a title alone on a plain background is better than a filler image.

It has been revealed that step 7: Build the reveals by hand. Demos, before-and-after comparisons, the key chart. These are the slides the audience will remember, and they need more care than a generator can give. See the section below.

Step 8: Break the layout rhythm deliberately. Make the two or three most vital slides look different: full-bleed image, a single enormous number, a black slide with one line of white text. Contrast is what makes a moment land.

Step 9: Rehearse with a timer. The slide count will be wrong in the first rehearsal. Cut, merge or split until the pacing matches the time.

It has been revealed that the opening. Not a title slide with your name and a logo while you say hello. Open on something that earns attention: a surprising number, a question, a screenshot of the problem, a single provocative sentence. Your name and affiliation can come on slide two, or be mentioned rather than shown.

The problem statement. One slide, one sentence, stays up while you explain why the audience should care. No bullets.

Industry observers note that the demonstration. If the talk has a demo, record it. Live demos fail in rooms with unreliable connections and unfamiliar projectors. A recorded demo with the audio off, narrated live, gives the same effect with none of the risk. If you must go live, have the recording ready as a fallback.

Recent findings suggest that the data. One chart per slide, one message per chart, the message in the title. Strip gridlines, legends and secondary series. Highlight the one line or bar that matters in colour and grey out the rest. Label directly. Type large enough to read from the back.

The “so what.” After the evidence, a slide that states what it means in one sentence. This is a hold slide; give it time.

The close. The one sentence you want them to repeat, alone on the final slide. Not “Thank you” or “Questions?”; those can be said. The last thing on screen while you take questions should be your point.

Because the slides are now sparse, two things need handling.

It has been revealed that first, the speaker notes must carry what you intend to say, in cue form: the key phrases, the number you must not forget, the transition to the next slide. The generator will have put the stripped bullet content there; edit it into cues rather than prose.

In a recent development, second, the shared deck. Attendees who download a sparse deck afterwards get little from it. Options: export with notes visible; publish a companion blog post or document; or build a second “reading” version with more text on each slide. Many speakers do the first and link to a post.

For a twenty-minute talk, fifteen to twenty-five slides is typical once hold and beat slides are counted. For a forty-five-minute talk, thirty to fifty. Build-up sequences of several quick beats inflate the count without inflating the time, which is fine. What is not fine is a deck of forty dense slides for twenty minutes; that is a talk that will run over and leave the audience behind.

Sources indicate that rehearse at least twice with a timer, once alone and once with a listener. Cut the content you rush. Nobody has ever complained that a talk finished two minutes early.

Lightning talks (five to ten minutes). Five to eight slides, almost all holds. One idea, one piece of evidence, one takeaway. Cut everything else.

Industry observers note that workshops and tutorials. More slides, more text, because attendees will refer back and follow along. The reading-deck rules apply more here; still, keep each step to one slide.

Panel contributions. Often no slides at all, or two or three for a specific point. Resist bringing a full deck.

Keynotes. Fewer slides, longer holds, more full-bleed images and single sentences. The speaker carries almost everything; the slides punctuate.

Industry observers note that remote talks. The screen is small and the audience is distracted. Larger type still, more frequent slide changes to hold attention, and a recorded demo is essential because screen-sharing a live one adds another failure point.

In a recent development, how much of the deck should the AI tool produce? The structural first draft: layouts, consistency, speaker notes populated. Expect to edit every slide and rebuild the key ones.

Sources indicate that is it acceptable to have slides with only a title? Yes, and it is often the strongest format for a spoken talk. The audience listens instead of reading.

Recent findings suggest that what about code on slides? Short excerpts only, in a large monospace type, with the relevant lines highlighted and the rest dimmed. Anything longer belongs in the companion post.

It has been revealed that should I use animations? Simple builds (revealing elements in sequence) help pacing. Transitions and effects distract. Keep to the former.

Industry observers note that how do I make the deck distinctive if I cannot design? Your material is what makes it distinctive: your screenshots, your data, your diagrams, your sentences. Design restraint plus real content beats decorated templates every time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills.

Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.

The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going.".

Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.

Recent findings suggest that he felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.

Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.

"I remarked to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair.".

Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.

Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.

"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to.".

What a coincidence! Or maybe not?

"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was.".

Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®.

🇵🇭 FilBench - Can LLMs Understand and Generate Filipino?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities.
  • That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.
  • We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities. For example, Filipinos are among the most active ChatGPT users globally, ranking fourth in ChatGPT traffic (behind the United States, India, and Brazil [1] [2]), but despite this strong usage, we lack a clear understanding of how LLMs perform for their languages, such as Tagalog and Cebuano. Most of the existing evidence is anecdotal, such as screenshots of ChatGPT responding in Filipino as proof that it is fluent. What we need instead is a systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in Philippine languages.

That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.

We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.

In a recent development, the FilBench evaluation suite contains four major categories–Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation–divided into 12 tasks. For example, the Classical NLP category includes tasks such as sentiment analysis, whereas Generation tasks include different aspects of translation. In order to ensure that these categories reflect the priorities and trends in NLP research and usage, we curate them based on a historical survey of NLP research on Philippine languages from 2006 to early 2024. (Most of these categories exclusively contain non-translated content to ensure faithfulness to the natural use of Philippine languages.).

Each of these categories provides an aggregated metric. To create a single representative score, we compute the weighted average based on the number of examples in each category, which we call the FilBench Score.

To simplify usage and set up, we built FilBench on top of Lighteval, an all-in-one framework for LLM evaluation. For language-specific evaluation, we first defined translation pairs from English to Tagalog (or Cebuano) for common terms used in evaluation such as "yes" (oo), "no" (hindi), and "true" (totoo) among others. Then, we used the provided templates to implement custom tasks for the capabilities we care about.

FilBench is now available as a set of community tasks in the official Lighteval repository!

By evaluating several LLMs on FilBench, we uncovered several insights into how they perform in Filipino.

Sources indicate that in the past few years, we have seen an increase in region-specific LLMs that target Southeast Asian languages (SEA-specific), such as SEA-LION and SeaLLM. These are open-weight LLMs that you can freely download from HuggingFace. We find that SEA-specific LLMs are often the most parameter-efficient for our languages, achieving the highest FilBench scores compared to other models of their size. However, the best SEA-specific model is still outperformed by closed-source LLMs like GPT-4o.

It has been revealed that building region-specific LLMs still makes sense, as we observe performance gains of 2-3% when continuously fine-tuning a base LLM with SEA-specific instruction-tuning data. This suggests that efforts to curate Filipino/SEA-specific training data for fine-tuning remain relevant, as they can lead to better performance on FilBench.

We also observe that across the four categories on FilBench, most models struggle with Generation capabilities. Upon inspecting failure modes in Generation, we find that these include cases where the model fails to follow translation instructions, generates overly verbose texts, or hallucinates another language instead of Tagalog or Cebuano.

The Philippines tends to have limited internet infrastructure and lower average incomes [3], necessitating accessible LLMs that are cost- and compute-efficient. Through FilBench, we were able to identify LLMs that are on the Pareto frontier of efficiency.

According to recent reports, in general, we find that open-weight LLMs, i.e., models that you can freely download from HuggingFace, are way cheaper than commercial models without sacrificing their performance. If you want an alternative to GPT-4o for your Filipino language tasks, then try Llama 4 Maverick!

We also make this information available in the HuggingFace space of the FilBench leaderboard.

We hope that FilBench provides deeper insights into LLM capabilities for Philippine languages and serves as a catalyst for advancing Filipino NLP research and development. The FilBench evaluation suite is built on top of Hugging Face's lighteval, allowing LLM developers to easily evaluate their models on our benchmark. For more information, please visit the links below:.

The authors would like to thank Cohere Labs for providing credits through the Cohere Research Grant to run the Aya model series, and Together AI for additional computational credits for running several open models. We also acknowledge the Hugging Face team, particularly the OpenEvals team (Clémentine Fourrier and Nathan Habib) and Daniel van Strien, for their support in publishing this blog post.

If you are evaluating on FilBench, please cite our work:.

TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks.
  • According to recent reports, two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments.
  • It has been revealed that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

According to recent reports, two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

It has been revealed that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:.

Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step intends by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

Success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

For each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:.

Sources indicate that game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

Harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

In a recent development, long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel plans as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

Dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is important as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

In a recent development, in closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn.
  • Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.
  • Sources indicate that the BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn.

Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.

Sources indicate that the BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.

In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software glitch.”.

The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.

Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.

If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA notes will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”.

JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

In a recent development, both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.

The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

According to recent reports, JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

According to recent reports, humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®.
