Smol2Operator: Post-Training GUI Agents for Computer Use

📅 23 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR: This work reveals how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder.
  • Industry observers note that graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision.
  • In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that TL;DR: This work reveals how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder. We release all training recipes, data-processing tools, resulting model, demo and datasets to enable full reproducibility and foster further research 🫡. Find the collection here.

Industry observers note that graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision. Developing models that see and interact with user interfaces enables AI agents to navigate mobile, desktop, and web platforms. This will reshape the future of digital interaction.

In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy. We demonstrate how to transform a model with zero grounding capabilities into an agentic coder capable of understanding and interacting with graphical interfaces.

Rather than aiming for a SOTA model, our goal is to demonstrate the entire process, from data processing to model training, and, in doing so, show how to unlock GUI-grounding capabilities in VLMs.

GUI capabilities combine understanding of the interface and precise element localization. These abilities enable the model to translate high-level tasks into low-level GUI actions such as clicking, typing, ….

Our approach leverages SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct as the baseline model, a small powerful vision-language model that initially has no grounding capabilities for GUI tasks. This makes it an ideal candidate to demonstrate the effectiveness of our training methodology. Through our two-phase training process, we first instill grounding capabilities in the model, then enhance it with agentic reasoning abilities using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

We evaluate our approach on an established perception benchmark: ScreenSpot-v2, which tests the model’s ability to understand and locate elements within screenshots. Our process is inspired by the AGUVIS paper, and we leverage their carefully curated datasets to build upon their foundational work.

Evolution of ScreenSpot-v2 performance during the training phase of the base model SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct.

In a recent development, this section explains how we convert heterogeneous GUI actions format from multiple datasets into a single unified format. By standardizing function names, signatures, and parameters, we create consistent, high-quality data that forms the foundation for effective model training.

One of the primary challenges when working with multiple GUI automation datasets is the lack of standardization in action representations. Different datasets use varying function signatures, parameter naming conventions, and action taxonomies, making it difficult to train a unified model across diverse data sources.

It has been revealed that we took the open-source datasets (xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2), originally used by AGUVIS, and implemented a comprehensive data transformation pipeline to create a unified action space. Our approach involved:.

Here are real examples from our action conversion system (preprocessing/action_conversion.py) showing how we transform heterogeneous action representations into our unified format (grounding coordinates normalized to [0,1]):.

Before (Original Action Dataset Formats):.

After (Unified Action Dataset Formats):.

This unification process was essential for creating coherent training data that allows the model to learn consistent action patterns across diverse GUI environments.

To maximize flexibility for different use cases, we developed the Action Space Converter (utils/action_space_converter.py), a tool that allows users to easily adapt from an action space to their own custom action vocabularies and naming conventions.

You can use this tool to transform one action signature (function names, parameter names, and parameter value changes, ...) into another:.

The Action Space Converter provides:.

This tool enables researchers and practitioners to:.

The Action Space Converter is particularly valuable for preparing datasets for training, as it ensures consistent action vocabularies across different deployment environments while maintaining compatibility with existing automation frameworks.

Sources indicate that through this pipeline, we transform the open-source datasets xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2 into our unified action space (see here). The output of this process is released as two new fully formatted datasets: smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 and smolagents/aguvis-stage-2.

According to recent reports, phase 1 leverages the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset, which introduces GUI grounding by pairing low-level instructions with diverse executable actions (expressed in code form). For example, a user/assistant turn in smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 follows the structure:.

Industry observers note that each sample links a screenshot with multi-turn user/assistant interactions, enabling the model to learn fine-grained action grounding across dialogue turns. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Before proceeding with full-scale Phase 1 training, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to determine optimal training configurations.

We experimented with different image sizes and coordinate representation systems to identify the optimal configuration for SmolVLM2:.

Some SOTA GUI VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL) appear also to use a different normalized range (0–1000), which was not tested in this experiment.

It has been revealed that table 1: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (400k samples, aguvis-stage-1). Higher is better.

Sources indicate that as demonstrated in our benchmark results, SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct base initially achieved 0% performance on perception benchmarks like ScreenSpot-v2. This complete lack of grounding capability provided us with a clean slate to evaluate the effectiveness of our training methodology.

From our experiments, we determined that:.

Using the optimal configuration (1152px resolution with normalized coordinates), we trained for 2 epochs on the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset. The results were remarkable, +41% improvement over baseline on ScreenSpot-v2.

This dramatic improvement demonstrates that our Phase 1 training successfully instilled fundamental grounding capabilities in the model, enabling it to understand and locate visual elements within screenshots.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

According to recent reports, whereas Phase 1 provided grounding capabilities, Phase 2 targets agentic reasoning, the ability to deliberate and plan before acting. This stage transforms the model from a reactive system identifying GUI elements into a proactive agent capable of executing complex, multi-step interactions.

Phase 2 uses the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 dataset, which introduces agentic scenarios:.

Explicit reasoning about upcoming actions.

Context consistency across multiple interaction steps.

High-level instructions require multi-step, low-level actions.

For example, the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 chat message is like this:.

In a recent development, each sample links a screenshot with a system/user/assistant turn. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Starting from the Phase 1 checkpoint (1152 px resolution, normalized coordinates), we fine-tuned the model for two epochs on smolagents/aguvis-stage-2. The accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 increased from 41% to 61%, indicating that explicit reasoning improves GUI grounding performance.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct after Phase 1 finetuning (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

All training code, data processing pipelines, datasets and model are open-source!

Our experiments demonstrate that high-quality, reasoning-oriented data can substantially improve GUI grounding, even for small VLMs, using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Beyond raw performance gains, these results show that the GUI grounding capabilities are largely determined by the quality of the data. Carefully curated datasets teach models the structure and semantics of user interfaces, providing the grounding needed for accurate action prediction.

To support the development of GUI agents, we’re open-sourcing everything: our complete pipeline, datasets, and trained model. You can reproduce our results, experiment with different models and architectures, or adapt our approach to new domains. The future of agentic AI depends on researchers like you pushing these boundaries further!

Sources indicate that while SFT excels at supervised tasks, emerging methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) help develop stronger reasoning capabilities and enable real-time adaptation. These advances point toward a fresh generation of GUI agents that learn and improve through interaction rather than relying solely on static datasets.

Let’s build the future of GUI agents together 🤗.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we released swift-transformers two years ago (!) with the goal to support Apple developers and help them integrate local LLMs in their apps.
  • We want to double down on the use cases that provide most benefits to the community, and lay out the foundations for the future.
  • swift-transformers is a Swift library that aims to reduce the friction for developers that want to work with local models on Apple Silicon platforms, including iPhones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we released swift-transformers two years ago (!) with the goal to support Apple developers and help them integrate local LLMs in their apps. A lot has changed since then (MLX and chat templates did not exist!), and we’ve learned how the community is actually using the library.

We want to double down on the use cases that provide most benefits to the community, and lay out the foundations for the future. Spoiler alert: after this release, we’ll focus a lot on MLX and agentic use cases 🚀.

swift-transformers is a Swift library that aims to reduce the friction for developers that want to work with local models on Apple Silicon platforms, including iPhones. It includes the missing pieces that are not provided by Core ML or MLX alone, but that are required to work with local inference. Namely, it provides the following components:.

Sources indicate that most of the time people use the Tokenizers or Hub modules, and frequently both. Some notable projects that rely on swift-transformers include:.

Version 1.0 signals stability in the package. Developers are building apps on swift-transformers, and this first major release recognizes those use cases and brings the version number in line with that reality. It also provides the foundation on which to iterate with the community to build the next set of features. These are some of our preferred updates:.

Version 1.0 comes with breaking API changes. However, we don’t expect major problems if you are a user of Tokenizers or Hub. If you use the Core ML components of the library, please get in touch so we can support you during transition. We’ll prepare a migration guide and add it to the documentation.

Here's how to use Tokenizers to format tool calling input for an LLM:.

For additional examples, please check this section in the README and the Examples folder.

Recent findings suggest that honestly, we don’t know. We do know that we are super interested in exploring MLX, because that’s usually the current go-to approach for developers getting started with ML in native apps, and we want to help make the experience as seamless as possible. We are thinking along the lines of better integration with mlx-swift-examples for LLMs and VLMs, potentially through pre-processing and post-processing operations that developers encounter frequently.

We are also extremely excited about agentic use in general and MCP in particular. We think that exposure of system resources to local workflows would be 🚀.

If you want to follow along in this journey or want to share your ideas, please contact us through our social networks or the repo.

We are immensely grateful to all the contributors and consumers of the library for your help and feedback. We love you all, and can't wait to continue working with you to shape the future of on-device generation! ❤️.

Many thanks to the Hugging Face team for the recognition and for pushing the Swift ecosystem forward. It’s been an honor to contribute Swift Jinja to the community, and I look forward to building the future together!♥️♥️♥️.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.

Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.

Sources indicate that every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.

According to recent reports, he illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

Industry observers note that on failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need significant-manufacturer controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.

In a recent development, for team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.

Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

高品質で多様なトレーニングデータなしに、日本文化を真に理解するAIを構築することはこれまでほぼ不可能でした。これを変えるため、NVIDIAは、日本の人口統計、地理的分布、文化的特性に沿ったペルソナを含む初のオープン合成データセット、Nemotron-Personas-Japan を公開しました。CC BY 4.0 ライセンスのもと提供される本データセットは、機微な個人データに依存することなく日本社会を反映した AI システム構築のための、プライバシー保護と規制対応を両立した基盤を提供します。.

NVIDIA のエンタープライズ向け合成データ生成システム、NeMo Data Designer を用いて作成されたNemotron-Personas-Japan は、すでに広く利用されている US Personas データセットの成功を機に日本版として開発されました。本リリースは、各国・地域におけるソブリン AI 開発を支援する合成ペルソナデータセットとデータ構築方法のグローバルコレクションの第一弾です。.

本データセットは、Nemotron モデルをはじめとするオープンソースの 大規模言語モデル(LLM) とシームレスに連携するよう設計されており、企業向けチャットボットから各種ドメインの AI エージェントに至るまで、日本語 AI アプリケーション向けのファインチューンを容易に行えるようになっています。.

NVIDIAの合成データ生成用マイクロサービスである NeMo Data Designer を用いて構築されています。この複合AIシステムは、複雑な Jinja テンプレート、Pydantic による検証、構造化出力、自動リトライ、および複数の生成バックエンドのサポートを可能にします。これらは、このような大規模な合成データセットの生成に必要なツール群です。さらに、以下のモデルも活用しています。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan は、日本の公的な人口統計および労働統計に整合するよう設計されると同時に、AI トレーニングにおいて重要な以下の点を考慮して生成されました：.

このデータセットには、個人を特定できる情報（PII）は一切含まれていません。年齢、名前、職業などは公的な統計データの分布に基づいていますが、存命・故人問わず、実在の人物と結びつくことはありません。全てのペルソナは完全に人工的に生成されているため、実際の文化的パターンを保ちながらも、個人のプライバシーを損なうことなくトレーニングに利用できます。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japanは、日本のソブリン AI システムを開発する日本のモデル開発者向けに設計されています。現在、LLM開発者が使用する訓練データのほとんどは英語であり、日本やインドなど各地域の開発者は、母国語で高品質なデータを入手するのに苦労しています。.

本データセットを含め、NVIDIA の Nemotron-Personas の一連の取り組みは、こうした課題を直接解決するものです。地域固有のニュアンスを捉えつつ、開発者が地域固有の言語で多様かつ複雑なデータを生成できるようサポートします。データセットは国勢調査データ、日本人の命名規則、文化的特徴など地域のコンテキストに基づき、すべて母語で生成しています。.

そのため、日本で自分たちのモデルの採用を拡大し、日本の文化的コンテキストを理解したい すべての AI モデルの開発者の方々のお役に立てれば幸いです。.

本データセットに含まれる合成ペルソナを以下のようなことに活用できます：.

AI 開発には、実世界の人々を反映した多様で高品質な訓練データへのアクセスが長らく課題でした。企業向け AI の開発はプライベートデータが主流となっており、研究者、スタートアップ、そして特に利用可能なデータが少ない地域のAI開発者にとって障壁となっていました。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan を CC BY 4.0 のもとで公開することで、企業レベルの高品質な合成データへのアクセスを可能とし、従来のコスト、プライバシーの懸念、地理的な制約といった障壁なしに、文化的背景を正確に反映した AI システムを誰でも構築できるようになりました。.

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People are trying to vibe code games.
  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
  • Industry observers note that first, what is vibe coding?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

Industry observers note that first, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

Sources indicate that however, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

Earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very swiftly.

To address this issue, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

It has been revealed that I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

In a recent development, I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

In a recent development, the official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

Recent findings suggest that roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

The unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Industry observers note that unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

In a recent development, this approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

Sources indicate that this will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

It has been revealed that here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

Industry observers note that so, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires users to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

Industry observers note that then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

Sources indicate that the engine is currently very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

It's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what's going on in the space!

I've been working on something along similar lines, called Rosh.

Recent findings suggest that it covers some of the things you list as missing. Rooms are multiplayer and live: people and AI agents can be in the same room changing it together. The same room works in real time in your browser (three.js), a terminal, Unity and Unreal Engine. It also reads the room back to the AI as text, with notes on what looks wrong, so agents can fix their own object placement etc.

Simple Sudoku Solver in Verilog

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Veitheller

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome back to another round of Simple Sudoku Solvers!
  • Verilog is a hardware description language.
  • Sources indicate that the solver is about 145 lines, plus 40 lines of ceremony to feed it a puzzle and print the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back to another round of Simple Sudoku Solvers! If you are unfamiliar with the series, I suggest you start with the first post or by perusing the backlog. Last time, in assembly, we told the CPU exactly what to do, one instruction at a time. Today we go one level lower and build the machine directly in Verilog.

Verilog is a hardware description language. You donât write a program that will at some point run on hardware. Instead, you describe a circuit, and the compiler turns that description into gates and flip-flops. Weâll run it in a simulator, because I donât have a Sudoku chip lying around (future work), but the solver is real hardware in the sense that a synthesis tool accepts it and tells us how many gates it would take. Still counts, even with sim2real TBD.

Sources indicate that the solver is about 145 lines, plus 40 lines of ceremony to feed it a puzzle and print the result. You can run it with iverilog -o sudoku sudoku.v && vvp sudoku, using Icarus Verilog. I didnât test it anywhere else. As always, the code is on GitHub.

Season three is about solvers, specifications, and constraints, and somehow also about hardware and the lowest of low levels. Thatâs because hardware is possibly the purest version of a specification (and, to be quite honest, because I felt like it).

So, whatâs cool about Verilog?

I think this was the strangest episode so far, for me. I donât mean that in a bad way.

If youâve never read Verilog before, here is what you need for this post.

According to recent reports, A module is a circuit with inputs and outputs. wire [8:0] x is a bundle of nine wires, numbered 8 down to 0. reg is a bit of a misnomer: itâs a value we assign in a procedural block, and whether it becomes an actual register is actually dependent on our usage of it.

Industry observers note that there are two kinds of blocks we care about. always @* describes combinational logic. Its outputs are a pure function of its inputs, and they change whenever the inputs do. Think of it as a very massive expression.

always @(posedge clk), on the other hand, describes sequential logic. It runs once at every rising clock edge, and the <= assignments inside it all happen together at the end of that edge. Thatâs where all our state lives.

Industry observers note that for loops exist, but in synthesizable code they are unrolled completely. A loop over 81 cells is 81 copies of its body. Keep that in mind, it will matter. Itâs also very cool, so itâs worth keeping in mind anyway.

The board is the same 81 cells as always, but since hardware doesnât really do arrays of bytes, it is one 324-bit vector, with four bits per cell and 0 for an empty cell:.

Industry observers note that we have three input wires and output regs (remember, not necessarily registers). Thatâs the whole interface of our chip.

We put a puzzle on the puzzle wires, hold start for one cycle, and wait until done goes high (think in currents). Then, if solved is set, board has the answer. Otherwise, the board is unsolvable.

Reading a cell is a slice, which we wrap in a small function.

Slices work like in many other languages, except that the operators +: and -: encode a direction from the start index. Here, we say âstart at 4 * i and take the next 4 bitsâ.

Units are the 27 rows, columns, and boxes we always care about. We describe them with a function that tells us which cell is the k-th member of unit u:.

The first 9 are the rows, then come the columns, and the icky expression at the end there is the box arithmetic with our usual set of magic numbers.

It has been revealed that fun fact: this looks like it does division at runtime, but it doesnât. We only ever call it with constants from unrolled loops, so the synthesis tool computes all of it ahead of time (much like an optimizing compiler would). What is left is just the wiring, and the box arithmetic decides which wires connect.

According to recent reports, like in many previous installments, we track digits as bitmasks. And like in our assembly episode, when itâs convenient we use the trick where digit d lives in bit d, and an empty cell lands in bit 0, which we throw away:.

Industry observers note that in hardware this is a decoder, four wires in, ten wires out, one of them lights up. Dropping bit 0 is just not connecting it. We donât need a branch, and in this case not even an instruction. These sorts of tricks are annoying the higher up the stack we go, but they come naturally to us when weâre thinking in circuits and currents.

We also need the opposite direction, from a single bit back to a digit, and a popcount:.

We are back to having to write our own popcount, regretfully, but it doesnât have to be smart. Itâs a chain of adders in the end, unrolled by our magical synthesis tool again.

This is where Verilog differs from everything else weâve done!

The following block is combinational. Every clock cycle, it looks at the whole board and computes, for all 81 cells at the same time, everything the solver could want to know.

Thatâs quite a few symbols, but it almost looks familiar I think.

It has been revealed that for each of the 27 units we or together the digits it contains into seen. While we do that, we check if a digit was already there, and if so, the unit has a clash. No other solver in the series has needed this check so far, and youâll see in a minute why we need it now. Hint: it has to do with the parallel nature of the system.

In a recent development, the candidates are the usual not-yet-taken numbers, and we compute them for all cells. We end up with four answers:.

Sources indicate that this reads much like the solver loop weâve written many times, but it works completely differently, because there is no loop. The circuit that is synthesized has 81 candidate calculators and a long chain of comparators for the minimum that are all settling at once.

It has been revealed that why the clash check? Here, because of parallelism, forced fills in every forced cell in the same cycle. If two cells in the same unit are both set to the same number, we write both of those in the same cycle and nothing checks at the end. Instead, we check the unit for duplicates at the next cycle, and treat a clash like any other unsolvable branch.

Recent findings suggest that so weâve successfully parallelized our work, including our mistakes! Fun!

Since there is no recursion, the search becomes a state machine with three states:.

RUN propagates and branches, BACK backtracks, and HALT is the stop condition.

Industry observers note that for backtracking we need a stack. The entry has the board before a guess, the cell we guessed in, and the candidates we havenât tried yet:.

It has been revealed that every guess fills at least one cell, so the search canât go deeper than 81, and 81 entries are enough to hold our search tree. Math! Logic!

Unfortunately, we have to pay for every entry in hardware, no matter if we end up using it or not.

Sources indicate that I originally called the second array cell, but it turns out cell is a reserved word in Verilog. Itâs used for configurations, which I had never heard of before. Shows what I know. Iâm just documenting this because where is a bit of an odd name, I think, but I didnât think to pull out the thesaurus1.

Anyway, time to look at the actual states.

Side note: the first cycle is spent initializing, then we fall through to our case structure.

According to recent reports, RUN is our whole solver as an if chain. If the board is dead, we backtrack. If there are forced cells, we fill all of them and come back next cycle to continue our work. If the board is full, weâre done and set HALT and all our stopping variables.

Sources indicate that otherwise we dance. pick is the candidate mask of the MRV cell:.

Recent findings suggest that we push the current board, the cell, and the remaining candidates, and then write the lowest candidate into the board. pick & -pick isolates the lowest set bit, and pick & (pick - 1) clears it, so together they split the mask into what to try now vs.Â what to try later. Thatâs my official favorite trick from the last episode making a second appearance as a subtractor and a row of and gates.

Industry observers note that this is also the place that tripped me up most when I was learning Verilog for this: all of these <= assignments happen together at the clock edge. We write board into the stack and change one cell of board in the same cycle, and the stack still gets the old board, because everything on the right-hand side was read before the edge. The timing is very explicit, and my intuitions are still very much developing.

The BACK state looks at the top of the stack:.

and then does one of three things:.

If the stack is empty, weâve tried everything, and there is no solution.

It has been revealed that if the top entry has no candidates left, we pop it and stay in BACK, so the next cycle looks at the entry below. So we do one backtracking step per cycle, at worst 81 times. This seems wasteful at first, but itâs actually beautiful in its simplicity I find.

Otherwise we restore the saved board, try the next candidate, and go back to RUN. The entry stays on the stack with one fewer candidate, ready to come back if this oneâs a dud, too.

Recent findings suggest that this, too, is the same copy-and-restore dance number from assembly, but itâs copying a board in one cycle. A register that is 324 bits wide is just 324 flip-flops that all load at the same time. If you design the board you can do whatever, it turns out.

It has been revealed that and thatâs it! Weâve solved the board!

Sources indicate that our usual hard puzzle takes 7,639 cycles. The puzzles from the repository take between 5 cycles (easy) and 411 cycles (evil), and a puzzle with two 8s in the first row is rejected in 2 cycles, because the clash check catches it right away.

That number is hard to compare with the other episodes. If the circuit ran at 1 MHz, 7,639 cycles would be about 7.5 milliseconds. But I havenât placed and routed it, so I donât know how fast it could really be made2. The 81 comparator chain we built above would probably be the limit, but again, I have no intuitions on how to measure this.

Recent findings suggest that the simulation, on the other hand, is slow. Icarus simulates every wire of that circuit on every cycle, and running the hard puzzle takes about 11 seconds on my machine. That makes it the slowest solver in the series by a wide margin, beating even Agda. Thatâs not a fair comparison, but I think itâs funny anyway, because we came to the land of speed and wires and ended up with the slowest simulations of the series.

As for size, I let the genie guide me and ran the solver through Yosys targeting Lattice iCE40, a family of small FPGAs that hobbyists like. It comes out at about 35,000 lookup tables and 28,000 flip-flops, almost all in the stack. That is a lot more than any iCE40 chip Iâve found has, so weâd need a bigger FPGA, or a stack in block RAM, which would cost us a cycle per access.

It has been revealed that if you want to build this circuit, be my guest! Do send pictures and/or measurements, though, please.

We built a Sudoku solver out of (simulated) wires and flip-flops, and made the thing nicely parallel. Through our little state machine, we also added a fresh tool to our bag of tricks. Time will tell if we need it again.

I still think this one fits the season better than it might have seemed on paper. We really did specify Sudoku in hardware, in a way, in a very lop-sided chip.

In the next episode, we stop writing search code entirely once again: we hand the constraints to z3 and let it find the answer for us, much like in Prolog and miniKanren, but differently. See you there!

According to recent reports, 1. We canât all be Kent Beck.

According to recent reports, 2. Synthesis turns the description into gates. Placing and routing then decide where on the chip each gate goes and how the wires run between them, and only then do you know how long a signal takes to get through the slowest path, which sets the maximum clock speed through the annoyances of physics. I didnât do that step by hand, and I donât know whether there is a tool for doing it automatically for me.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports.

Nov 24, 2026 12 min read.

Financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units. The process is sensitive, labor-intensive, and subject to strict deadlines. This article explains how non-deterministic Artificial Intelligence (AI) components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business, increases drafting and review speed, and maintains the quality of the final report.

A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units (such as the UK's National Crime Agency) to flag known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.

SARs should give a clear and concise explanation of the reason(s) for the suspicion, identifying:.

The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives organizes information from most to least important, much like a news article.

Because the structure moves from the broadest, most critical information down to the narrowest, a reader can grasp the core of the case from the opening lines alone and turn to the later sections only for supporting detail.

In the following system context diagram, a human agent views the investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then drafts the suspicious activity report. Once the report is reviewed by another peer, it is submitted to a financial intelligence unit.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

In the following diagram, there are 4 key timelines of any investigation:.

High-level diagram of a traditional reporting system (Source: authors).

We propose improving the traditional reporting system by using AI to automate selected tasks and generate high-quality SAR drafts, followed by specialized human review and minor edits where necessary. The goal is to increase throughput, reduce cost per case, and decrease reporting failures.

In the following system context diagram, human agent effort is shifted to review/edit the AI-assisted report drafting and review.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

In a recent development, we changed the earlier design to support background automation of suspicious activity report generation. As soon as the investigation is complete, the case is sent to the queue for processing by the Agentic System. Before the human agent picks the case for drafting the report, the AI Agent has drafted the first version to speed up the report generation.

High-level diagram of an AI-powered reporting system (Source: authors).

The non-deterministic nature of AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), creates two central concerns:.

The proposed solution is a multi-agent system, with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, and supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.

Industry observers note that grounding is the foundation of trustworthy SAR generation. The system should make it easier to state only what the evidence supports, not merely make the prose more fluent.

High-level diagram of the agentic system (Source: authors).

Sequence diagram of Drafter agent, Judge Agent and Human (Source: authors).

Industry observers note that quality means more than well-written prose. It means a complete, internally consistent, reviewable narrative that meets institutional and jurisdictional requirements.

Unlike traditional software, LLM outputs are non-deterministic, and "quality" is subjective. In the case of report writing, "what does a good report look like?" becomes more subjective. Hence, there is a need to test the "subjective" aspects against "objective" metrics, and here the Eval shines.

Evals are like tests of regular software development practices, and they can be leveraged in the following processes:.

There are a few broad focus areas where the model output has to be tested on a continuous basis:.

For example, Evals can be written to assess different aspects of the generated narrative like:.

Sample Eval can look like this:.

According to recent reports, once we have scores from all the evals, either we can use a weighted average or a simple average of all the individual scores to figure out the final grading criteria. This is how the Evals can be leveraged to grade the quality of generated output.

Sequence diagram of Evals grading (Source: authors).

It has been revealed that since the model and prompt are bound to change, this adds another dimension of non-determinism to the system. With any production system, we need to have a regression run of all evals against the golden data set before any model upgrade or prompt/config change happens.

Sources indicate that the golden data set has to be collected initially with different edge cases with defined input and output. This will help in testing the system during development. The Golden Data Set can be augmented with human feedback in production where they love the output generated by the AI system.

Evals shall answer some of the generated report’s quality metrics like :.

In a recent development, traditional testing is a deterministic process of verification - it asks, "Did we build the product right?" against a fixed specification. This approach fails when a system’s core logic is probabilistic, because non-deterministic output may be more likely to introduce subtle degradations of quality that do not result in explicit crashes and may not be repeatable. Hence, it is crucial to monitor the decision-making trajectory, from initial intent to final outcome.

The system is gradually improved by generating telemetry, understanding the system, and patching the underlying problems.

According to recent reports, human review remains a policy decision owned by the BSA/AML function. AI accelerates preparation; it does not replace accountable judgment.

In a recent development, treat models and prompts as regulated production changes. The release plane provides controlled progress rather than "ship and hope.".

The bottleneck in drafting a quality Suspicious Activity Report was qualified personnel. LLM-based systems can reduce that dependency, but only if they're engineered for it, with grounding and evals as the substitute for the judgment of a qualified investigator.

The mechanism we've described treats non-determinism as an engineering problem rather than an excuse. Grounding drafts in a case-specific knowledge graph and operational data keeps the Drafter Agent grounded in evidence. A Judge Agent and deterministic fact-checker turn "does this read well?" into measurable checks against factuality, completeness, and the Inverted Pyramid structure the FIU expects. Evals and a golden dataset give these subjective judgments an objective, regression-testable backbone, the same way unit tests do for deterministic code. And a release process that versions models, prompts, and configuration, gated with shadow/canary rollout and feature-flag rollback, treats every change to the system as a production release.

None of this shifts accountability away from the humans who own it. The BSA/AML officer still decides what gets filed; the agentic system's job is to make sure that when a human reviews a draft, the evidence is already assembled, the uncertain claims are flagged, and the reviewer's time goes to judgment rather than transcription. Risk-tiered routing means the system earns trust on familiar, low-risk cases before it is ever allowed near the ones that matter most.

SAR narratives can now be drafted at machine speed, by codifying what "good" looks like into evals a machine can check against. When a human reviews the output, they're not taking the narrative on faith; they can trace the reasoning and the evidence lineage behind it, and that traceability is what turns speed into trust.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security filed a final rule on November 23, 2026, adding Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and six other entities in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand to its export-control Entity List over the risk of diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or customers.

It has been revealed that the rule is scheduled for publication on November 25, 2026. It lists three entities under Malaysia, three under Singapore and one under Thailand. BIS determined that they present a significant risk of being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end owners.

Each listing requires a license for all items subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), with license applications reviewed under a presumption of denial. The Entity List also limits most license exceptions for exports, reexports and in-country transfers when a listed entity is a party to the transaction.

The Malaysian additions are MSFusion Sdn. Bhd., PT Megaspeed International and Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd. Singapore’s entries are Apex Enterprise Solutions (Singapore) Private Limited, Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and Swiftdata Pte. Ltd., while Megaspeed (Thailand) Co., Ltd. is the Thai addition.

Sources indicate that megaspeed International’s Singapore entry lists Megaspeed, Megaspeed International, 7Road International and 7Road International Pte. Ltd. as aliases. The Thailand entry also carries the 7Road International and 7Road International Pte. Ltd. aliases, identifying alternative names associated with the listed business.

The End-User Review Committee decides Entity List additions by majority vote. Commerce chairs the committee, which also includes representatives of the State, Defense and Energy departments and, where appropriate, the Treasury Department.

Sources indicate that the applicable standard is reasonable cause, based on specific and articulable facts, to believe an entity has been involved, is involved or poses a significant risk of becoming involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security or foreign-policy interests. BIS issued the rule without prior notice and comment under authority provided by the Export Control Reform Act.

A savings clause covers qualifying shipments that were already en route under actual orders on November 23. Those shipments may continue under their previous license-exception or no-license-required eligibility if completed within 30 days after public inspection. The clause applies only to shipments already underway; new orders do not receive a general 30-day transition.

It has been revealed that the action follows a joint statement from the Commerce and Justice departments on November 17, 2026, that disclosed the Megaspeed investigation timeline. Commerce noted it initiated the investigation in 2024 after proactive monitoring identified suspicious activity involving potential sensitive-semiconductor diversion. Investigators requested Nvidia records about direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025. That month, BIS agents and Singaporean law-enforcement officials conducted an on-site end-use check and interviewed then-CEO Alice Huang. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in the criminal investigation.

Sources indicate that the new designations make the identity of every party in a covered transaction central to export compliance. Unlike an individual supplier’s no-sell decision, the Entity List applies a federal licensing requirement and presumption of denial across all items subject to the EAR, giving the listings consequences beyond one chipmaker’s relationship with Megaspeed.

Accelerating Qwen3-8B Agent on Intel® Core™ Ultra with Depth-Pruned Draft Models

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

Qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

It has been revealed that speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

In a recent development, before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

The speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Our recent work demonstrates that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

It has been revealed that the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

It has been revealed that to showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

In a recent development, here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. This simple workflow highlights just a fraction of the possibilities unlocked when accelerated Qwen3 models meet frameworks like 🤗smolagents, bringing practical, efficient AI agents to life on AI PC. Try it here 🚀.

The response notes the recordings include at least one meeting between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, plus meetings on 12 dates from September 9 to September 28, 2026, in the executive conference room where a hidden device was later discovered. Many appear likely to contain confidential trade-secret material, including discussions with customers or about customer needs and OpenAI capabilities, while OpenAI identified others as containing material protected by attorney-client privilege.

In a recent development, alfozan was arrested on October 9, 2026, and later indicted on a single Wiretap Act count alleging that he concealed a recording device in the conference room to intercept oral communications. He pleaded not guilty on November 6, 2026.

Prosecutors described dozens of apparent AI-generated transcripts accompanying some recordings. The collection included 15 date-based subfolders covering September 8–28, 2026, with filenames identifying subjects such as AI-safety research, product activation and a sovereign bilateral briefing. The files appeared to have been categorized by date and renamed according to their contents.

Industry observers note that the response says records received from OpenAI show that Alfozan used Codex, the company’s productivity agent, in September 2026 to help configure the recording device and transmit and store audio through Dropbox. Examples include a September 27, 2026, prompt concerning a passphrase and firmware for a XIAO ESP32 device, the same kind OpenAI found inserted into a television three days later. A September 29, 2026, prompt requested voice detection with the goal of recording only speech.

Alfozan received a September 28, 2026, email notifying him that he had deleted 5,026 Dropbox files, according to the response. His browsing history showed repeated Dropbox access on October 5, 2026, for a project associated with the recordings. Those records indicate that audio was transmitted through or stored in the cloud account, as well as kept locally on his personal computer.

Separately, prosecutors mentioned investigators found cellphone photographs of every page of a printed document marked confidential that appeared to be a strategic-partnership term sheet between OpenAI and another tech giant. An OpenAI attorney signed it on August 13, 2026. Metadata and items visible in some photographs suggested they were taken at Alfozan’s home early on October 5, 2026, the same day a hidden camera recorded him looking for the device in an OpenAI conference room. The evidence developed so far strongly suggests that Alfozan recorded many meetings he neither attended nor had authority to attend, without notice to or authorization from OpenAI.

Alfozan’s November 20, 2026, motion argues that changed circumstances justify release: he faces only the Wiretap Act count, prosecutors have acknowledged finding no fresh evidence to support charges of trade-secret theft or acting as an unregistered foreign agent, and the vast majority of the recordings apparently contain random noise and silence. He proposed a $1 million bond secured by $500,000 of his own cash and up to $500,000 in unsecured promises from three sureties. He also gave the FBI his cellphone password on November 17, 2026, after a power failure at an FBI facility left the device locked.

Industry observers note that prosecutors countered that Alfozan remains a serious flight risk because of his financial resources, termination from OpenAI, uncertain U.S. employment prospects and personal and professional ties to Saudi Arabia. His wife, infant son, parents and siblings reside there.

The response describes WhatsApp communications with Saudi officials and a royal-family member, an October 6, 2026, invitation to join Echelon, a Riyadh-based AI and technology organization, a 16-minute WhatsApp call on October 8, 2026, and a Saudi trip planned for October 12, 2026. Those details are part of the government’s detention argument; the indictment remains limited to the Wiretap Act count.

The government claims how Alfozan used or intended to use the recordings remains under investigation and that the absence of evidence on those questions so far is not a changed circumstance justifying release.

Prosecutors asked the court to keep Alfozan detained or, alternatively, impose a significant secured bond, a travel restriction, location monitoring and other pretrial conditions, including a bar on contacting OpenAI personnel and accessing or transmitting OpenAI materials. The proposed OpenAI restriction reflects concern that he could retain cloud access to confidential information, including the recordings.

The renewed release request was scheduled for a November 24, 2026, hearing before Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse, and the court docket lists jury selection and trial for January 20, 2027. The release decision will test whether conditions can address both flight risk and the government’s concern about continued access to confidential OpenAI material.

Tech Report: Introducing RTEB: A New Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a newly introduced benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • The performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a newly introduced benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

The performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

This is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on latest, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following issues:.

Sources indicate that the Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

Because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to upcoming problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

Misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these concerns are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a fresh, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

This hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

In a recent development, A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We plan to continually patch both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an issue on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we blueprint to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest newly introduced datasets, find issues in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an problem in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our plans for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

The RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the fresh Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

[1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Industry observers note that is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (at the moment denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

The discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets shows why a single retrieval average can hide notable differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

RTEB leaderboard have bm25 and some other baseline models https://leaderboard.mteb.org/benchmark/RTEB(beta)?pin=mteb%252Fbaseline-bm25s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DXC Technology declared the launch of DXC Frontier Code Assurance on November 24, 2026, a managed cybersecurity service that uses Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to find, validate and help remediate vulnerabilities in mission-critical software. The service is available immediately, with DXC specialists retaining responsibility for deciding which findings warrant action.

It has been revealed that claude Mythos identifies potential vulnerabilities, after which DXC cybersecurity specialists validate the results, rank them by business impact and decide the remediation path. Customers receive a prioritized roadmap with auditable evidence at each step, and DXC then helps them remediate and patch. DXC indicates the service can find flaws that traditional scanners miss.

CEO Raul Fernandez explained the emphasis on remediation rather than alert volume in DXC’s October 30, 2026 earnings call: “A scan that produces every alert at once creates a backlog, not security.” The launch release argues that as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, the bottleneck shifts toward prioritizing and executing fixes, making the validation and remediation workflow central to the offer.

It has been revealed that organizations can start with a single application and expand over time, or fold the service into ongoing security operations. It sits within DXC’s global cybersecurity practice, which runs 12 Security Operations Centers across more than 40 countries with thousands of cybersecurity professionals.

Recent findings suggest that fernandez noted the offer combines DXC’s existing cyber incident detection, rapid response and recovery management with Mythos-based vulnerability discovery and detection. The managed component is therefore broader than generating scan results: it links model-led discovery to an established security-delivery organization and to patching support.

The November 24 announcement followed an earlier market release. On the same October 30 call, Fernandez said DXC had recently received approval to productize Claude Mythos into Frontier Code Assurance, had released it to market in late October 2026 and was already selling it. The new release is therefore a formal launch announcement for an offering that had already been offered for sale, rather than a first disclosure of availability.

Fernandez also described the service as able to scan 10 million lines of code quickly, document vulnerabilities and create a patching framework, with DXC products helping customer teams apply the fixes.

It has been revealed that frontier Code Assurance builds on the multi-year global alliance announced by DXC and Anthropic on June 11, 2026. The agreement made DXC a Global Premier partner in the Claude Partner Network. The companies mentioned they would train tens of thousands of forward-deployed, Claude-certified engineers and builders to work inside customer environments, with cybersecurity among the initial focus areas.

It has been revealed that the operational question is whether that human-supervised handoff can absorb the additional findings produced by AI discovery. DXC’s model puts validation, business-risk ranking and an auditable remediation trail between Mythos and changes to mission-critical software, making completed fixes the relevant measure of the service’s work.
